name: Classic-Style Test 3
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer in the style and difficulty of recent LSATs. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: Swim coach: Sports scientists warn that teenage swimmers who train more than twenty hours a week face a higher risk of serious shoulder injury than those who train less. But this warning is overblown. Throughout high school I trained more than twenty-five hours a week, often in two sessions a day, and I never injured a shoulder once.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the swim coach's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: attacks the motives of the sports scientists rather than addressing the evidence on which their warning is based
takes for granted that what is true of competitive swimmers must also be true of athletes in other sports
treats one person's experience as sufficient to show that a claim about increased risk is exaggerated
fails to consider that the coach may have trained fewer hours in high school than the coach now remembers
concludes that heavy training is beneficial merely because it caused no harm in a single case
questions.explanation: A warning about higher risk says injuries are more likely, not certain, so one swimmer who escaped injury does nothing to show the risk is overstated; (C) names this anecdote-versus-general-claim flaw. (D) is tempting but merely possible: nothing suggests the coach misremembers, and accurate memory wouldn't rescue the argument anyway. (E) treats 'not harmful' as 'beneficial,' a conclusion the coach never draws.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The scientists' warning about shoulder injuries in heavy-training teen swimmers is overblown.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The coach trained 25+ hours a week in high school and never hurt a shoulder.

breakdown.analysis: So what if the coach never got hurt? A higher risk means more injuries across many swimmers, not an injury for every single one. This is the anecdote-vs.-general-claim flaw; it's a classic, know it. It's like saying seatbelt warnings are overblown because your cousin never wore one and never got hurt. We need an answer that says the coach uses one case to dismiss a claim about likelihood.

choices.note: The coach never mentions the scientists' motives. Wrong flaw.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The scientists who issued this warning are paid by a physical therapy company, so we can ignore what they say.

choices.note: There's no jump to other sports anywhere in the argument. Right topic, wrong group.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Heavy training never hurt my shoulders as a swimmer, so it won't hurt the shoulders of pitchers or tennis players either.

choices.note: CORRECT. The coach's own injury-free career is the entire evidence, and a risk claim is about how often injuries happen across many swimmers. One case can't show that the risk is exaggerated.

Tempting, because it hints that the coach's story might be unreliable. But it's merely possible: nothing suggests the coach misremembers, and even with perfect memory one swimmer can't refute a claim about risk.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: I'm sure I studied four hours a night in college, so four hours a night is clearly enough to get top grades.

choices.note: The coach says the warning is overblown, not that heavy training is good for you. 'Didn't hurt' isn't 'helped.' This answer invents a conclusion.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Skipping breakfast never made me sick, so skipping breakfast must be good for your health.

questions.stimulus: Horticulturist: Many gardeners in dry regions spread pale gravel over the soil around their shrubs, believing that the gravel helps the shrubs conserve water. In fact, the practice usually does more harm than good. Pale gravel reflects sunlight onto the shrubs' leaves, raising leaf temperatures, and warmer leaves lose more water than the gravel saves by slowing evaporation from the soil.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the horticulturist's argument?
choices: Pale gravel reflects sunlight onto the leaves of nearby shrubs and so raises the temperature of those leaves.
Gravel spread over the soil around shrubs slows the evaporation of water from the soil beneath it.
Gardeners in dry regions should stop growing shrubs that need large amounts of water to survive.
Spreading pale gravel around shrubs usually does more harm than good to the shrubs.
Shrubs surrounded by pale gravel lose more water through their leaves than do shrubs surrounded by bare soil.
questions.explanation: The gardeners' belief is background; the horticulturist's position is that the practice 'usually does more harm than good' (D), and the facts about reflected sunlight and leaf water loss are the reasons offered for it. (E) and (A) restate those reasons, and (C) adds a recommendation the argument never makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Spreading pale gravel around shrubs usually does more harm than good.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Pale gravel reflects sunlight onto the leaves and heats them; warmer leaves lose more water than the gravel saves at the soil.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The first sentence is the popular view, which is background. 'In fact, the practice usually does more harm than good' is the author's own claim, and the last sentence explains why. So the last sentence supports the second, and nothing supports the last sentence. We need an answer that matches the second sentence.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's a big chunk of the stimulus. But it's a premise: it's offered to explain why the practice backfires.
This is a fact the horticulturist concedes in passing ('than the gravel saves by slowing evaporation'). It's support material, not the point.
The horticulturist never says anything about which shrubs to grow. This adds a recommendation the argument doesn't make.
CORRECT. Everything after 'In fact' supports this claim: the reflected heat and the extra water loss are the reasons the practice does more harm than good.
Close to the last premise, and it's the step that sets up the conclusion. But it's still a reason. The argument uses it to show the practice is harmful; it isn't the claim being argued for.

questions.stimulus: Last spring, the Marrow Creek trail, alone among the six trails in the Ashgrove nature preserve, had its trailhead signs replaced with new signs asking hikers to stay on marked paths. Over the summer, rangers recorded 40 percent fewer instances of hikers leaving the Marrow Creek trail than they had the summer before. The new signs, therefore, reduced off-trail hiking there.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: On the preserve's other trails, whose signs were unchanged, recorded off-trail hiking was about the same as the previous summer.
Several hikers interviewed on the Marrow Creek trail last summer said that they had not noticed the new signs.
Rangers spent fewer hours patrolling the Marrow Creek trail last summer than they had the summer before.
A heavy storm closed the Marrow Creek trail for most of July, though the preserve's other trails stayed open.
Trampling by hikers is the leading cause of damage to plants along trails in nature preserves of this kind.
questions.explanation: To credit the signs, the argument needs the drop not to have happened anyway; (A) shows that comparable trails without new signs saw no drop over the same summer, which rules out preserve-wide causes. (C) and (D) weaken by offering other reasons for fewer recorded incidents, and (B) suggests the signs went unnoticed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new signs reduced off-trail hiking on the Marrow Creek trail.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Only Marrow Creek got new signs; recorded off-trail incidents there fell 40 percent from the previous summer.

breakdown.analysis: Before and after, with one change in between. So what else changed? Maybe the whole preserve had a rainy summer and fewer visitors. The argument doesn't tell us what happened on the other trails, which are the natural comparison group. We need an answer that rules out an alternative cause, ideally by showing that trails without new signs didn't see the same drop.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the comparison group. If off-trail hiking held steady where the signs didn't change, a preserve-wide cause (weather, fewer visitors, a new rule) is unlikely to explain the drop on Marrow Creek, which points to the signs.
This cuts the wrong way: if hikers didn't notice the signs, it's harder to believe the signs changed their behavior. And it's only 'several' hikers.
This weakens. Fewer patrol hours means fewer chances to record off-trail hiking, so the 40 percent drop could be a drop in observations rather than in hiking.
Another weakener. With the trail closed for a month, there were fewer hikers to wander off it. That's an alternative cause for the drop.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. It says why off-trail hiking matters, not whether the signs reduced it.

questions.stimulus: Two years ago, Brightwater Hospital introduced a checklist that nurses complete with every patient before discharge. Since then, the share of Brightwater's patients who are readmitted within thirty days of discharge has fallen substantially. Yet the regional health board, which monitors readmissions at every hospital in the region, still describes Brightwater's readmission rate as unacceptably high.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Completing the checklist takes nurses about fifteen minutes for each patient who is discharged from the hospital.
Before the checklist, Brightwater's readmission rate was nearly double the regional average, and it remains well above that average.
Some of the patients readmitted since the checklist was introduced had been discharged without the checklist being completed.
Administrators at several other hospitals in the region regard Brightwater's checklist as a model worth copying in their own wards.
Patients discharged using the checklist report greater satisfaction with their care than patients discharged before the checklist did.
questions.explanation: 'Fallen substantially' is relative to Brightwater's own past, while 'unacceptably high' is an absolute judgment; if the rate started at nearly twice the regional average, a big drop can still leave it too high (B). (C) is merely possible and doesn't show why the overall rate is still judged high. (A) and (E) are about time and satisfaction, not the rate.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Brightwater's readmission rate has fallen substantially, but the health board still calls it unacceptably high.

breakdown.analysis: Is a big drop the same as a low rate? No. Watch the switch from a relative word (fallen) to an absolute one (high). If you start very high, you can fall a lot and still be high, like a runner who cuts ten minutes off a marathon and still finishes last. We need an answer that shows Brightwater started far enough above the standard that it's still above it.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Nurses' time says nothing about why a falling rate would still be judged too high.

CORRECT. 'Fallen substantially' is measured against Brightwater's own past; 'unacceptably high' is measured against a standard. Starting at nearly double the average, the rate can fall a lot and still be too high.
Tempting, because it hints the checklist isn't always used. But it doesn't explain why the board still calls the overall rate too high; we don't know how many such patients there were.
This praises the checklist, which only deepens the puzzle about why the board is unhappy.
Satisfaction isn't readmission. Wrong dimension.

questions.stimulus:
Odile: The Halvard Museum should start charging admission. A modest fee would pay for longer opening hours, and at other museums that introduced such fees, attendance barely changed.

Tomas: Overall attendance might well hold steady. But free admission is what brings in families from the low-income neighborhoods around the museum, and even a modest fee would keep many of them away. The museum should stay free.
questions.stem: Odile and Tomas disagree over whether
choices: a modest admission fee would bring in enough money to pay for longer opening hours
overall attendance at the Halvard Museum would drop sharply if an admission fee were introduced
families from the neighborhoods around the museum value it more than its other visitors do
the Halvard Museum should begin charging visitors a modest admission fee
the museum's duty to nearby neighborhoods outweighs every other consideration in setting its policies
questions.explanation: Odile says the museum should charge admission and Tomas says it should stay free, so they disagree on (D). (B) is the trap: Tomas concedes overall attendance might hold steady. Tomas never addresses (A), neither speaker addresses (C), and (E) is far stronger than anything Tomas says.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Odile: Charge a modest fee; it would fund longer hours, and attendance barely changed at other museums that did this.; Tomas: Overall attendance may hold, but a fee would keep away low-income families nearby; stay free.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Look for the claim both speakers explicitly take sides on. Odile's conclusion is 'should charge'; Tomas's is 'should stay free.' Note the concession: Tomas agrees overall attendance might hold steady. That's the classic trap, a topic both mention but don't fight about.

choices.note: Odile says it would, but Tomas never addresses the money at all. To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no.
Tempting, since attendance comes up in both speeches. But Tomas concedes that 'overall attendance might well hold steady,' so he doesn't oppose Odile here.
Neither speaker compares how much different visitors value the museum. Tomas talks about access, not value.
CORRECT. Odile says the museum should start charging; Tomas says it should stay free. That's a direct yes/no split.
Too strong. Tomas thinks the effect on nearby families matters here, but he never says it outweighs everything, and Odile never takes a stand on it.

questions.stimulus: At Fennick Software, no code change is merged into the company's main codebase unless at least one engineer other than its author has reviewed it. In addition, every change that affects the payment system must be approved by a security lead before it is merged. Last week, a change that Imani wrote for the search page was reviewed by a colleague and merged.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Any merged change that was not approved by a security lead does not affect the payment system.
Imani's change to the search page was approved by a security lead before it was merged into the codebase.
Every change that has been reviewed by an engineer other than its author is eventually merged into the main codebase.
Imani's change to the search page did not affect the company's payment system in any way.
Changes that affect the payment system are reviewed more carefully than changes that do not affect it.
questions.explanation: The second rule says payment-system change AND merged → security-lead approval; its contrapositive is that a merged change without that approval doesn't affect the payment system, which is (A). (D) is tempting, but nothing says a search-page change can't touch the payment system. (C) reverses the first rule: review is required for merging, not enough for it.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Merged → reviewed by someone other than the author; 2. Affects payment AND merged → security-lead approval first; 3. Imani's search-page change was reviewed and merged.

breakdown.analysis: Write the rules as arrows. Merged → reviewed. Payment change merged → approved by a security lead. Contrapositive of the second for merged changes: not approved → not a payment change. Imani's change adds little: we know it was reviewed and merged, but not whether it touched payments. Watch for answers that reverse a rule or assume what a search-page change can't do.

choices.note: CORRECT. Rule 2: affects payment AND merged → approved by a security lead. Contrapositive for merged changes: not approved → doesn't affect payment. This is just the rule turned around.
We don't know this. Approval is required only for payment-system changes, and nothing says Imani's change touched the payment system.
This reverses Rule 1. Review is required for merging (necessary), not a guarantee of merging (sufficient).
Tempting, because it's a search-page change. But nothing says a search-page change can't touch payments; if it did, it was simply approved by a security lead too. Not guaranteed.
The rules say who must sign off, not how carefully anyone reviews. This adds a comparison the facts don't support.

questions.stimulus: In Tessaly's city council election this fall, turnout fell from 41 percent of registered voters to 33 percent, its lowest level in two decades. This was the first council election since the city, to save on printing and postage, stopped mailing a sample ballot to every household. Clearly, the city's decision to stop mailing sample ballots reduced turnout.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: Most residents who received sample ballots in earlier elections read them carefully before going to vote.
Turnout in Tessaly's council elections is generally lower than turnout in its elections for mayor.
The money the city saved by not mailing sample ballots was less than the value of the turnout it lost.
No resident who received a sample ballot in the previous council election failed to vote in that election.
Turnout in this fall's election would not have fallen as far had the city continued to mail sample ballots.
questions.explanation: To say the decision reduced turnout, the argument must assume the drop wouldn't have happened anyway; if turnout would have fallen just as far with sample ballots, the decision caused nothing (E). (A) is tempting but too strong: even if only some residents read the ballots, the decision could still have lowered turnout. (D) is far too strong, and (C) shifts to cost.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Stopping the sample-ballot mailing reduced turnout.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Turnout fell from 41% to 33% in the first council election after the mailing stopped.

breakdown.analysis: So what if the drop came right after the change? Maybe turnout would have fallen anyway: a dull race, bad weather, no contested seats. This is a counterfactual cause: to blame the decision, the argument needs the outcome not to have happened without it. We need a defender: an answer saying turnout wouldn't have dropped as much if the ballots had kept coming.

choices.note: Too strong. Even if only some residents read the ballots, losing them could still have lowered turnout. Negating it does no damage.
choices.negation: It's not the case that most residents who received sample ballots read them carefully.

choices.note: Irrelevant comparison. Council turnout versus mayoral turnout says nothing about why council turnout fell.
choices.negation: Council turnout is not generally lower than mayoral turnout.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. The argument is about whether the decision reduced turnout, not whether it was worth it.
choices.negation: The money saved was at least as great as the value of the lost turnout.

choices.note: Far too strong, and beside the point. The argument doesn't need perfect turnout among ballot recipients.
choices.negation: At least one resident who received a sample ballot didn't vote in the previous election.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: turnout would have fallen just as far even with sample ballots. Then the decision changed nothing, and the causal conclusion collapses.
choices.negation: Turnout would have fallen just as far even if the city had kept mailing sample ballots.

questions.stimulus: Researchers fitted forty red squirrels in Alder Wood with tracking collars and recorded where the squirrels foraged from September through November. During that period, the squirrels spent about 70 percent of their foraging time within twenty meters of a hazel tree. Clearly, the red squirrels of Alder Wood prefer to forage near hazel trees rather than elsewhere in the wood.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Red squirrels in most other woodlands spend the bulk of their foraging time near oak trees rather than hazels.
Hazelnuts are among the most nutritious foods available to red squirrels during the autumn months.
About 75 percent of the area of Alder Wood lies within twenty meters of at least one hazel tree.
Some of the collared squirrels spent even more of their foraging time near hazel trees in spring than in autumn.
Tracking collars can slightly reduce the distance that a squirrel travels while foraging in a single day.
questions.explanation: A preference means squirrels forage near hazels more than chance would predict, so the argument needs a baseline: how much of the wood is near a hazel. If 75 percent of the wood is, then spending 70 percent of the time there shows no preference (C). (B) strengthens, and (E) is merely possible and doesn't say which way any bias would run.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Alder Wood's red squirrels prefer to forage near hazel trees.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Collared squirrels spent about 70% of autumn foraging time within 20 meters of a hazel.

breakdown.analysis: Is 70 percent a lot? Only compared with something. If almost the whole wood is near a hazel, 70 percent is what you'd expect from squirrels that don't care at all. It's a missing comparison group: like saying people prefer shopping on Main Street because 70 percent of purchases happen there, when 90 percent of the shops are there. We need an answer that shows the 70 percent is no more than chance.

choices.note: Other woodlands aren't Alder Wood. Squirrels can prefer hazels here and oaks elsewhere, depending on what grows where.
This strengthens. It gives squirrels a reason to prefer hazels.

CORRECT. This is the missing baseline. If 75 percent of the wood is near a hazel, a squirrel foraging at random would spend about 75 percent of its time there. Spending 70 percent shows no preference at all.
This doesn't hurt. If anything it suggests the hazel attraction is consistent, and it's about a different season.
Merely possible, and directionless. Shorter trips don't tell us whether the squirrels end up closer to hazels or farther from them.

questions.stimulus: It is widely believed that feeding birds in winter makes them dependent on feeders and less able to find natural food. But in a three-year study of black-capped chickadees, birds with access to feeders still got most of their winter food from natural sources, and when the feeders were removed, those birds survived the rest of the winter at the same rate as birds that had never used feeders. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: chickadees that use feeders in winter gradually lose much of their ability to find food on their own
at least for chickadees, winter feeding does not appear to create the dependence that many people fear
winter feeding actually improves chickadees' chances of surviving long and unusually cold winters
people need not be concerned about any of the effects that feeding might have on wild birds
chickadees prefer the natural foods they find to the seeds that people offer at feeders
questions.explanation: The study cuts against the popular dependence worry, but only for chickadees, so (B) is properly limited. (A) restates the popular view the author is rejecting. (C) treats 'no worse off' as 'better off,' and (D) stretches one species and one worry into 'any effects' on 'wild birds.'

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Popular belief: winter feeding makes birds dependent; 2. Fed chickadees still got most food from natural sources; 3. Without feeders, they survived as well as never-fed birds.

breakdown.analysis: The author sets up a popular view and then brings evidence against it, so the blank should push back on that view, but no further than the evidence goes. The evidence is about chickadees and about dependence. We need an answer that says, roughly, 'feeding doesn't seem to make chickadees dependent.' Watch for answers that repeat the popular view or overreach to all birds.

choices.note: This is the popular view the author is pushing back on. The study points the other way.

CORRECT. The study shows fed chickadees kept foraging naturally and survived just as well without feeders, which cuts against dependence. The 'at least for chickadees' qualifier keeps it within the evidence.
The study found the same survival rate, not a better one. 'No worse off' isn't 'better off.'
Too broad. One species and one worry (dependence) can't clear 'any effects' on 'wild birds.'
Tempting, since fed birds still ate mostly natural food. But that could reflect availability, not preference, and it isn't the point the argument is building toward.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A city should waive the permit fee it normally charges for a street festival if the festival is open to the public free of charge, does not close any street served by a public bus route, and either is organized by a neighborhood association or gives all of its proceeds to a registered charity.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?
choices: The city should waive the fee for the Dorset Avenue block party, a free public event organized by the Dorset neighborhood association that will close a street on the number 4 bus route.
The city should not waive the fee for the Riverside Jazz Walk, a free public event that closes no bus route, because it is run by a private promoter who keeps the proceeds.
The city should waive the fee for the Elm Park Arts Market, which closes no bus route and is run by the Elm Park neighborhood association, although visitors must pay to enter.
The city should waive the fee for the Grove Street Food Festival, a free public event that closes no bus route, because its organizers expect it to draw large crowds downtown.
The city should waive the fee for the Larch Street Harvest Fair, a free public event that closes no bus route and that will give all of its proceeds to a registered charity.
questions.explanation: The principle says: free AND no bus-route closure AND (neighborhood association OR all proceeds to charity) → waive the fee. (E) meets every condition through the charity half of the 'or.' (A) is the tempting trap: it has the association but closes a bus route. (B) uses the principle to justify refusing a waiver, which it can't do.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: If a festival is free and open to the public, closes no bus-route street, and is either run by a neighborhood association or gives all proceeds to charity, then the city should waive its permit fee.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the judgment where every condition is met and the verdict is 'waive the fee.'

breakdown.analysis: This is a checklist: 1. free and public; 2. no bus-route street closed; 3. neighborhood association OR all proceeds to charity. The verdict it can deliver is only 'waive.' So the right answer must say 'waive' and satisfy all three. Each trap misses exactly one, or tries to get a 'don't waive' verdict out of a rule that only tells you when to waive.

choices.note: Tempting: free, public, and run by a neighborhood association. But it closes a street on a bus route, so a required condition fails and the principle doesn't apply.
The principle only says when the fee should be waived. It never says when the fee must be charged, so it can't justify 'should not waive.' This treats a sufficient condition as a necessary one.
Fails the first condition: the event isn't free to the public.
Meets the first two conditions but neither half of the 'either/or': no neighborhood association, no charity. Crowd size isn't part of the principle.
CORRECT. Free and public: yes. No bus-route street closed: yes. Either/or: all proceeds to a registered charity, yes. Every condition is met, so the principle says waive the fee.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Supporters of ranked-choice voting claim that it reduces negative campaigning. Their evidence is a single city where televised attack ads declined sharply after the system was adopted there. But attack ads declined nationwide that same year, even in cities that kept their old voting systems, so that city's experience proves nothing. Ranked-choice voting, therefore, does not reduce negative campaigning.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the columnist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: treats the failure of the supporters' evidence to establish their claim as showing that the claim is false
attacks the motives of the supporters of ranked-choice voting rather than the evidence that they offer for their claim
relies on nationwide figures that may not reflect conditions in the particular city the supporters cite
presumes, without providing justification, that negative campaigning is harmful to voters and to the candidates
concludes that ranked-choice voting is undesirable merely because it fails to achieve one of its intended goals
questions.explanation: The columnist shows that the supporters' evidence is weak, which at most leaves their claim unproven; concluding that ranked-choice voting does not reduce negative campaigning treats a failed argument as a disproof (A). (C) is merely possible and would quibble with the rebuttal rather than identify the leap to the conclusion. (E) adds a conclusion about desirability that the columnist never draws.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ranked-choice voting does not reduce negative campaigning.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Supporters' only evidence is one city's drop in attack ads; attack ads dropped nationwide that year, so that city proves nothing.

breakdown.analysis: Fine, the supporters' evidence is weak. Does that make their claim false? No. 'You haven't proven it' is not 'it's false.' Rebutting an argument isn't the same as proving the opposite; it's a classic, know it. It's like saying: your only witness was unreliable, so the defendant definitely didn't do it. We need an answer that says the columnist treats lack of proof as disproof.

choices.note: CORRECT. The columnist shows the supporters' evidence is weak, which at most leaves their claim unproven. Concluding the claim is false treats a failed argument as a disproof.
The opposite of what happens: the columnist goes straight at the evidence and says nothing about motives.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Supporters of ranked-choice voting are mostly consultants who profit from new election systems, so their claims can't be trusted.

choices.note: Tempting, but merely possible, and it's a quibble with the columnist's rebuttal, not the leap to the conclusion. Even if the rebuttal holds, the conclusion still overreaches.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Nationwide, house prices rose last year, so prices in our small town must have risen too.

choices.note: The columnist never says whether negative campaigning is good or bad. The argument is only about whether the system reduces it.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: This rule will reduce attack ads, so it will make voters better informed.

choices.note: The columnist never calls ranked-choice voting undesirable. This adds a conclusion about whether the system is good overall.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The new bus line didn't cut traffic as promised, so the city should never have built it.

questions.stimulus: After the Calloway ferry line put faster new vessels into service in March, the average time a ferry needed to cross the bay fell by six minutes. Yet in the months since, a larger share of the line's ferries have arrived late at their destination docks than did so in the months before the new vessels entered service.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain how the line's ferries could be arriving late more often even though their crossing times have fallen?
choices: Fares on the ferry line were raised slightly in March to help pay for the purchase of the new vessels.
Ferries on other lines that cross the same bay have also arrived late more often since March.
When the new vessels entered service, the line revised its timetable, cutting each scheduled crossing time by ten minutes.
Fog occasionally forces the ferries to slow to a crawl for several minutes in the middle of the bay.
Owners of private boats complain that the new ferries' larger wakes have made crossing the bay more difficult.
questions.explanation: 'Late' is measured against the timetable, not against the old crossing time; if the schedule was cut by ten minutes while actual crossings got only six minutes faster, the ferries are quicker than before yet more often behind schedule (C). (D) is tempting, but nothing says fog has become more frequent. (B) concerns other lines.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The ferries cross six minutes faster on average, but more of them arrive late than before.

breakdown.analysis: Faster but later? What does 'late' mean? Late compared with the schedule. If the schedule changed, a faster ferry can still miss it. It's like a teacher who moves a deadline up two days: you finish a day sooner than last year and still turn it in late. We need an answer that changes the yardstick, or otherwise shows how faster crossings and more late arrivals can both be true.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Fares don't affect when a ferry arrives.
So? This spreads the puzzle to other lines without explaining it. And other lines didn't get faster vessels, so their lateness may have nothing to do with ours.

CORRECT. 'Late' is measured against the timetable. If the schedule now allows ten fewer minutes but the ferries are only six minutes faster, they're quicker than before and still behind schedule more often.
Tempting, because fog causes delays. But nothing says fog got more common since March, and occasional fog was already part of the old crossings.
This is about private boats, not about the ferries' arrival times. Wrong group.

questions.stimulus: Of the patients at Corrigan Memorial Hospital who developed infections after surgery last year, 60 percent had been given a pre-operative antiseptic wash made with the hospital's new formula rather than its old one, which the hospital still uses for some patients. Clearly, the new formula does little or nothing to prevent post-surgical infections.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the argument?
choices: How much more does a wash made with the new formula cost the hospital than one made with the old formula?
Did any of the patients who were given the new formula report skin irritation after their pre-operative wash?
What percentage of post-surgical infections at other hospitals in the region are successfully treated with antibiotics?
Were most of the patients who developed infections after surgery last year given antibiotics before their operations?
What percentage of all the hospital's surgical patients last year were given a wash made with the new formula?
questions.explanation: The 60 percent figure means nothing without knowing how common the new wash was among all surgical patients: if 95 percent received it, the washed patients were underrepresented among infections and the formula looks effective; if 40 percent did, it looks ineffective (E). (D) is tempting, but it describes only the infected group again and gives no comparison between washed and unwashed patients.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new antiseptic formula does little or nothing to prevent post-surgical infections.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 60% of patients who got infections had been given the new-formula wash.

breakdown.analysis: Is 60 percent a lot? Only compared with how many patients got the new wash in the first place. If nearly everyone got it, 60 percent is low. This is a percentage-without-a-base-rate problem; it's a classic, know it. We need a question about the share of all surgical patients who got the new wash.

choices.note: Cost isn't effectiveness. Wrong dimension.
Side effects don't tell us whether the wash prevents infection.
Treatment after infection elsewhere has nothing to do with prevention here.
Tempting, since antibiotics affect infection. But it describes only the infected group again; it gives no comparison between patients who got the new wash and those who didn't.

CORRECT. If 95 percent got the new wash, then new-wash patients make up a smaller share of infections than of patients, and the formula looks effective. If only 40 percent got it, it looks worse than useless. Either answer changes how we judge the argument.

questions.stimulus: Textile cooperative director: We will sell the new Glenmorrow tartan blanket in our shop only if it can be woven entirely from wool produced on our members' farms. The tartan's crimson stripe takes the correct shade of dye only on wool from Kerran sheep, and none of our members raises Kerran sheep. So the Glenmorrow blanket will not be sold in our shop.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the director's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: If the Glenmorrow blanket could be woven entirely from members' wool, it would be sold in the cooperative's shop.
The Glenmorrow blanket cannot be woven without a crimson stripe of the correct shade.
Some of the cooperative's members could begin raising Kerran sheep within the next few years.
If the cooperative had Kerran wool, it would be able to weave the Glenmorrow blanket with its crimson stripe.
Wool from Kerran sheep costs considerably more than wool from the breeds that the cooperative's members raise.
questions.explanation: The premises show members' wool can't carry a correct-shade crimson stripe, but the conclusion needs that stripe to be required for the blanket; (B) supplies that necessary condition, so the blanket can't be woven entirely from members' wool and won't be sold. (D) is the trap: it gives the sufficient version, which leaves open weaving the blanket without the stripe. (A) reverses the 'only if' rule.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Glenmorrow blanket will not be sold in the shop.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Sold → woven entirely from members' wool; correct-shade crimson stripe → Kerran wool; no member raises Kerran sheep.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it. Sold → all members' wool. Correct stripe → Kerran wool. Members have no Kerran wool, so members' wool can't give a correct stripe. But who says the blanket needs the correct stripe? That's the gap. Add: blanket → correct stripe. Now: blanket from members' wool → correct stripe → Kerran wool, which members don't have. So no blanket from members' wool, so not sold. We need an answer linking the blanket to the stripe, in the necessary direction.

choices.note: This reverses the 'only if' rule. Knowing when the blanket would be sold doesn't help prove it won't be.
CORRECT. Then the blanket needs a correct-shade stripe, which needs Kerran wool, which no member produces. So it can't be woven entirely from members' wool, and by the rule it won't be sold.
If anything this opens a path to selling the blanket later. It doesn't help prove the conclusion.

Tempting: it links Kerran wool to the blanket. But it's the sufficient version (Kerran wool → can weave). The argument needs the necessary version: no correct stripe → no blanket. This leaves open weaving the blanket some other way.
Cost isn't part of the argument's rule. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Historian: Some scholars argue that the town of Korby must have been poor in the 1600s, because its parish records list very few bequests of silver. But in that period, families who owned silver plate typically gave it to their children while still living, precisely to avoid the heavy tax that was levied on bequests. So the scarcity of recorded bequests may say more about how Korby's wealthy families avoided taxes than about the town's poverty.
questions.stem: The historian's argument proceeds by
choices: arguing that the parish records are unreliable because the officials who compiled them had a stake in the tax on bequests
offering an alternative explanation for the evidence on which the scholars base their conclusion about the town
presenting new evidence that the town of Korby was in fact wealthy during the 1600s
questioning the scholars' expertise in interpreting the parish records of the seventeenth century
showing that the scholars' conclusion is inconsistent with other claims those scholars have made about the town
questions.explanation: The scholars infer poverty from few silver bequests; the historian points out that wealthy families gave silver away before death to avoid a bequest tax, which explains the same evidence without poverty (B). (C) is too strong: the historian never claims Korby was wealthy. (A) is wrong because the historian doesn't question the records' accuracy.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The scarcity of silver bequests may reflect tax avoidance rather than poverty.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Families with silver typically gave it to their children while living, to avoid a heavy tax on bequests.

breakdown.analysis: What does the historian actually do? Not dispute the records, not prove Korby rich. The historian takes the scholars' own evidence (few silver bequests) and gives another reason it would look that way. That's the alternative-explanation move. We need an answer that describes offering a different explanation for the same evidence.

choices.note: The historian never questions the records' accuracy. The records may be perfectly accurate; the point is what they mean.
choices.example: Example of this method: The tax collectors kept these records, and they profited from low counts, so the records can't be trusted.

choices.note: CORRECT. The scholars read 'few silver bequests' as poverty; the historian says it could reflect families handing silver down early to dodge a tax.
Tempting, but too strong. The historian never says Korby was wealthy, only that the bequest records don't show it was poor.
choices.example: Example of this method: Korby's tax rolls show more large farms than any nearby town, so Korby was in fact wealthy.

choices.note: Nothing is said about the scholars' qualifications. The historian attacks their inference, not them.
choices.example: Example of this method: These scholars are economists, not historians, so their reading of old records counts for little.

choices.note: The historian never cites anything else the scholars have said.
choices.example: Example of this method: These scholars say Korby was poor, yet they also say it built three new churches in the 1600s.

questions.stimulus: At the start of last quarter, the software team at Pemberton Systems began requiring that every code change be accompanied by automated tests. Over that quarter, the number of bugs reported by the team's customers fell by 30 percent from the previous quarter. So the testing requirement is reducing the number of bugs that the team's customers encounter.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Most engineers on the team say that writing the required tests has considerably slowed their work on new features.
Customer-reported bugs fell by a similar percentage last quarter at several companies that have no testing requirement.
Automated tests can catch some kinds of bugs that manual reviews of code by other engineers tend to miss.
The drop in reported bugs came almost entirely from parts of the software changed after the requirement took effect.
Several customers who had reported many bugs in the previous quarter stopped using the team's software before last quarter.
questions.explanation: If the decline is concentrated in code written under the new requirement, the improvement tracks the requirement rather than a general cause such as fewer customers or an industry-wide trend (D). (C) is the tempting trap: it says only that tests 'can' catch 'some' bugs, which makes the mechanism possible without showing it worked here. (B) and (E) supply alternative explanations and so weaken.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The testing requirement is reducing the bugs customers encounter.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The requirement began last quarter; customer-reported bugs fell 30% from the quarter before.

breakdown.analysis: Before and after again. So what else might explain the drop? Fewer customers reporting, an industry-wide improvement, a quiet quarter with fewer releases. The best strengthener pins the effect to the cause. Here, the requirement applies only to changes made after it started, so if the drop shows up only in that code, the link is much tighter. We need an answer that matches the effect to where the cause operated, or rules out an alternative.

choices.note: Speed isn't the issue. This is about a cost of the requirement, not whether it reduced bugs.
This weakens: if bugs fell just as much without the requirement, something else (an industry-wide trend) may explain the drop.
Tempting, because it describes a mechanism. But 'can catch some kinds' only makes the effect possible; it doesn't show that the requirement caused this drop.
CORRECT. The improvement shows up exactly where the requirement applied, which ties the drop to the tests rather than to a general cause like fewer customers or an industry trend.
This weakens. Losing heavy reporters is an alternative reason that reported bugs fell.

questions.stimulus: Urban ecologist: To shade its new boulevards within a few years, the city plans to line them exclusively with fast-growing poplars. This plan is shortsighted. Poplars are short-lived, and their brittle limbs often break in storms, so the city would likely have to replace most of the trees within twenty years. Slower-growing oaks, by contrast, would shade the boulevards for well over a century.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the ecologist's argument by the claim that the city would likely have to replace most of the trees within twenty years?
choices: It is the overall conclusion of the argument, which each of the other claims in the argument is offered to support.
It is a premise offered in support of the claim that poplars are short-lived and that their limbs often break.
It is supported by another claim in the argument and in turn supports the argument's main conclusion.
It describes a consequence of the city's plan that the ecologist argues is unlikely to actually occur.
It is offered as evidence that slower-growing oaks would shade the boulevards for more than a century.
questions.explanation: The replacement claim is drawn from the facts about poplars' short lives and brittle limbs, and it in turn supports 'This plan is shortsighted,' so it is a subsidiary conclusion (C). (A) is the trap: the claim is flagged by 'so,' but it supports a further claim, so it isn't the overall conclusion. (B) reverses the support relation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The city's poplars-only plan is shortsighted.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Poplars are short-lived and brittle, so most would need replacing within 20 years; oaks would shade for over a century.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. 'Short-lived, brittle' → 'replace within twenty years' → 'shortsighted.' The 'so' tempts you to call the replacement claim the conclusion, but it is itself used to support 'This plan is shortsighted,' which nothing else props up. So the claim is in the middle: supported and supporting. We need an answer that says it gets support and gives support to the main conclusion.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's flagged by 'so.' But it isn't the end of the line: it is itself used to show the plan is shortsighted. The main conclusion is 'This plan is shortsighted.'
Backward. The short life and brittle limbs support the replacement claim, not the other way around.
CORRECT. It's drawn from the facts about short life and brittle limbs ('so'), and it's a reason the plan is shortsighted. That makes it a subsidiary conclusion.
The ecologist thinks this consequence is likely, not unlikely. It's a reason against the plan.
Right claim, wrong relation. The oak lifespan is a separate premise; the replacement claim doesn't support it.

questions.stimulus: Last season, runners on the Westfield High track team who attended the coach's optional sessions reviewing race footage cut their race times by more, on average, than did runners who skipped the sessions. So, to improve the team's race times this season, the coach plans to require every runner on the team to attend the film sessions.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Some runners who have skipped the film sessions would improve more if they attended them.
The film sessions are the most valuable part of the team's entire training program.
Every runner who attended the sessions cut his or her race times by more than every runner who skipped them.
Requiring attendance will not make the sessions less enjoyable for the runners who already attend them voluntarily.
The film sessions take up less of the runners' time each week than their weight-training sessions do.
questions.explanation: Runners who already attend will keep attending, so the plan can improve the team only through those who now skip; if none of them would improve more by attending, requiring attendance gains nothing (A). (D) is tempting but shifts from race times to enjoyment, and its negation doesn't defeat the plan. (B) and (C) are far stronger than the argument needs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Requiring all runners to attend the film sessions will improve the team's race times.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Last season, attendees improved more on average than those who skipped.

breakdown.analysis: Who chose to attend? Maybe the most motivated runners, who'd have improved anyway. For the plan to work, forcing the skippers in has to help at least some of them; the attendees were already going. We need a minimal, hedged answer: at least some skippers would benefit.

choices.note: CORRECT. Runners who already attend will keep attending, so the plan can help only through those who now skip. Negate it: none of the skippers would improve more by attending. Then requiring attendance gains nothing.
choices.negation: None of the runners who have skipped the sessions would improve more by attending them.

choices.note: Too strong. The sessions can help without being the most valuable thing the team does. Negating it doesn't hurt the plan.
choices.negation: The film sessions are not the most valuable part of the training program.

choices.note: Far too strong. The argument relies on averages; some overlap between the groups is fine.
choices.negation: At least one runner who attended didn't improve more than every runner who skipped.

choices.note: Tempting, because a forced session might feel different. But the goal is race times, not enjoyment; less enjoyable sessions could still improve times. Negating it doesn't sink the plan.
choices.negation: Requiring attendance will make the sessions less enjoyable for current attendees.

choices.note: Irrelevant comparison. The plan's success doesn't depend on how the sessions compare in length with weight training.
choices.negation: The film sessions take up at least as much time as weight training.

questions.stimulus: Engineer: Stone arch bridges built in the Calden region during the 1700s are, on average, in noticeably better structural condition today than stone arch bridges built there in the early 1900s, even though the older bridges have had nearly two more centuries in which to deteriorate. Evidently, Calden's eighteenth-century bridge builders followed sounder construction practices than did their twentieth-century successors.
questions.stem: The engineer's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: overlooks the possibility that most poorly built bridges from the earlier period have long since collapsed or been replaced
takes for granted that a bridge in good structural condition is also safe for the traffic it now carries
fails to consider that builders in the earlier period may have constructed far fewer bridges than later builders did
draws a general conclusion about construction practices from the condition of the bridges in a single region only
treats the age of a bridge as though it were the main factor determining the bridge's present condition
questions.explanation: Only the 1700s bridges that are still standing can be compared today; if most poorly built ones from that era have already collapsed or been replaced, the survivors are an unrepresentative sample of eighteenth-century work (A). (E) is tempting because age is mentioned, but the engineer treats age as a handicap the older bridges overcame, not as the cause of their condition. (D) misdescribes a conclusion that is explicitly limited to Calden.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Calden's 1700s bridge builders used sounder construction practices than its early-1900s builders.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Surviving 1700s stone bridges are, on average, in better condition than early-1900s ones, despite being older.

breakdown.analysis: Which 1700s bridges are we looking at? Only the ones still standing. The weak ones fell down or were torn out long ago. That's survivorship bias: the sample is filtered by the very quality being measured. It's like saying old cars were better built because the 1960s cars you see on the road today run great; the bad ones are in the scrapyard. We need an answer that says the surviving older bridges may not represent all the bridges built back then.

choices.note: CORRECT. Only the 1700s bridges that survived can be inspected today. If the badly built ones are gone, the survivors are the cream of their era, and comparing them with all early-1900s bridges proves nothing about typical practices.
The engineer never talks about safety or traffic. This answers a question the argument doesn't raise.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The bridge passed its structural inspection, so it can certainly handle the heavier trucks that will use it next year.

choices.note: So? How many bridges each era built doesn't tell us how well each bridge was built, and the comparison uses averages.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our town built more houses in the 1950s than in the 1850s, so 1950s builders must have been less careful.

choices.note: The conclusion is limited to Calden's builders. There's no generalization beyond the region.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Calden's old bridges are sound, so eighteenth-century builders everywhere used sound methods.

choices.note: Tempting, because age is mentioned. But the engineer uses age only to say the older bridges did well despite it; the argument credits construction practices, not age.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: This bridge is the oldest in the county, so it must be the one in the worst condition.

questions.stimulus: Bakery owner: A customer recently asked us to bake a cake bearing a message that mocked a local charity, and we declined. Some say that a business should fill any lawful order, but our refusal was justified. The cake was to be displayed at a public event in a box bearing our bakery's name, and people there would reasonably have taken the message to reflect our own views.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the bakery owner's reasoning?
choices: A business should fill every lawful order it receives unless filling that order would cause the business to lose money on the sale.
A business may refuse a lawful order if the item would publicly bear its name and would reasonably be read as its view.
A business should not be held responsible for the views expressed in items that it makes at a customer's request.
A business that declines a customer's order should always explain its reasons for doing so to that customer in writing.
A message that most people at a public event would find offensive should not be displayed at that event at all.
questions.explanation: The owner's grounds are that the cake would be publicly tied to the bakery and reasonably read as the bakery's own view; (B) turns exactly those facts into permission to decline. (E) is tempting, but it governs what may be displayed at events, not what a bakery may refuse to make. (C) cuts against the owner by denying that the bakery bears responsibility for the message.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bakery was justified in refusing the order.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The cake would be displayed publicly in a box with the bakery's name, and people would reasonably take the message as the bakery's view.

breakdown.analysis: A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says, triggered by the facts the arguer gives. Facts: public display, bakery's name, reasonably read as the bakery's view. Conclusion: refusing was justified. So we want: if an item would publicly carry the business's name and look like its view, the business may refuse.

choices.note: Under this principle the bakery should have filled the order, since nothing suggests it would have lost money. It cuts against the owner.

CORRECT. The owner's facts are exactly these: the cake would be publicly displayed in a box with the bakery's name, and people would reasonably read the message as the bakery's. This principle turns those facts into permission to refuse.
This cuts against the owner, whose whole reason is that people would hold the bakery responsible for the message.
This is about how to refuse, not whether refusing was justified.
Tempting, since the message mocked a charity. But it governs what events may display, not what a bakery may refuse to make, and the owner never says most people would find the message offensive.

questions.stimulus: Campaign strategist: In last year's city council races in Marbury, the 20 candidates whose volunteers knocked on the doors of more than 5,000 households during the campaign won 15 seats, while the 30 candidates whose campaigns reached fewer households won only 6 seats. So door-to-door canvassing substantially improves a candidate's chances of winning a council seat.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the campaign strategist's argument?
choices: Several of the candidates whose campaigns visited more than 5,000 households lost their races by very wide margins.
Door-to-door canvassing costs a campaign considerably more per voter reached than does advertising sent by mail.
The candidates whose campaigns reached fewer households spent more, on average, on television advertising than the others did.
Campaigns already leading in early polls attract the most volunteers, who determine how many households a campaign can visit.
In council races in neighboring cities last year, the link between canvassing and winning was weaker than in Marbury.
questions.explanation: (D) shows the correlation could run backward: candidates already favored to win attract volunteers, and volunteers are what let a campaign reach many households, so being a frontrunner explains both the canvassing and the wins. (E) is tempting, but a weaker link elsewhere is still a link. (C) strengthens by ruling out greater ad spending as the explanation, and (A) is already built into the 15-of-20 figure.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Door-to-door canvassing substantially improves a candidate's chances of winning.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Heavy-canvassing candidates won 15 of 20 races; lighter-canvassing candidates won 6 of 30.

breakdown.analysis: Correlation, then a causal conclusion. So which came first? Maybe strong candidates canvass more, rather than canvassing making candidates strong. Reversed causation (or a common cause); it's a classic, know it. It's like noticing that restaurants with long lines serve good food and concluding the lines make the food good. We need an answer showing that likely winners are the ones able to canvass heavily.

choices.note: Already built into the numbers: 5 of those 20 lost. A few big losses don't undercut a pattern of 15 wins in 20.
Cost isn't the issue. Canvassing can be expensive and still raise a candidate's chances.
This actually strengthens: it rules out bigger ad budgets as the reason the canvassing candidates won.

CORRECT. This shows the correlation could run the other way: being a frontrunner brings volunteers, volunteers make heavy canvassing possible, and frontrunners also tend to win. Canvassing may just be a marker of strength.
Tempting, but a weaker link elsewhere is still a link, and it tells us nothing about why the link held in Marbury.

questions.stimulus: Any city whose transit system runs trains at least every ten minutes during rush hour will see its rush-hour train ridership rise from year to year. Rush-hour train ridership in Ashcombe has been rising steadily in each of the past five years. So Ashcombe's transit system must be running its trains at least every ten minutes during rush hour.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Any museum that offers free admission on weekends will see its weekend attendance rise. Weekend attendance at the Corbin Museum has not risen. So the Corbin Museum must not be offering free admission on weekends.

Every hospital in the region that adopted electronic charts last year reduced its paperwork costs. So electronic charts will reduce paperwork costs at any hospital in the region that adopts them in the future.

Any choir that rehearses each piece at least six times will perform it without major errors. The Westbrook Choir rehearsed its new piece eight times. So the Westbrook Choir will perform the new piece without major errors.
Most candidates endorsed by the Ledger newspaper win their elections. Pelham has been endorsed by the Ledger this year. So Pelham will certainly win the election that she is now contesting.
No restaurant whose chef trained at the Lyon Institute fails to earn a top rating from critics. Hollis Bistro earned a top rating from critics. So its chef must have trained at the Lyon Institute.
questions.explanation: The argument has the form: frequent trains → rising ridership; ridership is rising; so trains are frequent, which affirms the consequent. (E)'s double-negative premise ('no restaurant whose chef trained at Lyon fails to earn a top rating') just means Lyon training → top rating, and it then infers the training from the rating, the same error. (A) is the trap: it looks closest on the surface but reasons validly by contrapositive. (C) is also valid, while (B) and (D) commit different errors.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ashcombe's trains run at least every ten minutes at rush hour.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Trains every ≤10 minutes → ridership rises; Ashcombe's ridership is rising.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: If A, then B; B; so A.

breakdown.analysis: Arrow it: frequent trains → ridership rises. We're told ridership rises, and the argument concludes frequent trains. That's the reversal: the result could have other causes (new housing near stations, higher gas prices). Find the answer with If A → B; B; so A. Watch for the valid look-alike that uses the contrapositive, and decode double negatives: 'No X fails to Y' means every X is Y.

choices.note: Tempting: it's the closest on the surface. But it reasons by contrapositive (no rise → no free admission), which is valid. The original is flawed, so this doesn't match.
A different flaw: generalizing from past cases to all future ones. No conditional is reversed.
Valid: the condition is met, so the result follows. The original affirms the result instead.
A different flaw: it turns 'most' into 'certainly.' The original's problem is direction, not a quantifier.
CORRECT. Decode the double negative: chef trained at Lyon → top rating. Then it sees a top rating and infers Lyon training. Same error: affirming the consequent.

questions.stimulus: Last season, the Arden Theater began selling any seats still unsold on the day of a performance at half the regular price. The theater sells no other discounted tickets, and its regular price has not changed. Compared with the season before, the theater sold 4 percent fewer regular-price tickets last season, yet its total revenue from ticket sales was exactly the same.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choices: Some patrons who had previously bought regular-price tickets waited last season to buy half-price tickets instead.
Most of the people who bought half-price tickets last season had never attended the Arden Theater before.
The total number of tickets the theater sold was greater last season than in the season before.
The theater's performances last season were attended by fewer people than its performances the season before.
Selling unsold seats at half price on the day of a performance increased the theater's total ticket revenue.
questions.explanation: Revenue held steady while regular-price sales fell 4 percent, so half-price sales replaced the lost revenue; since each half-price ticket earns half as much, the theater had to sell twice as many half-price tickets as the regular tickets it lost, so total tickets rose (C). (A) is the tempting cannibalization story, but nothing shows any patron switched. (E) is contradicted by the flat revenue.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. New: unsold seats sold at half price on the day of the show; 2. No other discounts; regular price unchanged; 3. Regular-price sales fell 4%; 4. Total ticket revenue unchanged.

breakdown.analysis: Do the arithmetic with easy numbers. Say 100 regular tickets at $20 before: $2,000. Last season, 96 regular tickets: $1,920. Revenue is still $2,000, so half-price tickets brought in $80, which at $10 each is 8 tickets. Total: 96 + 8 = 104 tickets, more than 100. Hard to prephrase beyond that, so watch for answers that tell a plausible story the numbers don't require.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the familiar story about discounts cannibalizing full-price sales. But the 4 percent drop could have other causes; nothing shows these patrons switched.
We don't know who bought the half-price tickets. Possible, but unsupported.

CORRECT. Revenue stayed flat while regular sales fell 4 percent, so half-price sales made up that lost revenue. Each half-price ticket brings in half as much, so the theater needed twice as many half-price tickets as the regular tickets it lost. Total tickets went up.
The facts point the other way: more tickets sold overall means more seats filled, not fewer.
Contradicted. Total revenue was exactly the same as the season before.

questions.stimulus: The Halberd Foundation will fund the new science wing at Corrin Academy only if the academy first raises matching funds from its alumni. The academy can raise such funds only if it hires a full-time fundraising director, and the academy's board has voted not to hire one. So the Halberd Foundation will not fund the new science wing.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: The ferry will run on Sunday only if the harbor is clear of ice, and the harbor will be clear of ice only if the thaw continues through Saturday. The thaw is continuing. So the ferry will run on Sunday.
The festival will be held in Ward Park unless it rains on Saturday, and the weekend forecast calls for heavy rain on Saturday. So the festival will not be held in Ward Park this year.
The council will approve the proposed skate park only if most nearby residents support it. A survey shows that most nearby residents oppose the skate park. So the council will not approve it.

Marla will be promoted only if she completes the certification course. She can complete it only if her manager approves time off, and her manager has refused to approve it. So Marla will not be promoted.

Any student who completes the honors seminar earns extra credit, and any student who earns extra credit qualifies for the Dean's Award. Jun did not complete the honors seminar. So Jun will not qualify for the award.
questions.explanation: The argument chains two necessary conditions (funding → matching funds → fundraising director) and denies the last one to conclude no funding; (D) does exactly the same with promotion → course → approved time off. (A) affirms the necessary conditions instead, (E) denies the first sufficient condition, and (C) has only one link.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Halberd Foundation will not fund the science wing.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Funding → matching funds raised → full-time fundraising director hired; the board voted not to hire one.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A only if B; B only if C; not C; so not A.

breakdown.analysis: Arrow it: Fund → match → director. No director, so no match, so no funding. That's a valid contrapositive chain. Match the skeleton, not the topic: two 'only if' links, the last condition denied, a definite 'will not' conclusion. Traps either reverse the arrows, deny the wrong end, or drop a link.

choices.note: Same chain of 'only ifs,' but it reasons the wrong way: meeting a necessary condition doesn't guarantee the result. The original denies the last condition; this one affirms it.
Different structure: one condition, not a chain, and it moves from a forecast to a certain conclusion.
Tempting: valid and it ends in 'will not.' But it uses a single 'only if,' not a two-link chain.
CORRECT. Promoted → completes course → time off approved. Time off refused, so no promotion. Same two-link chain, same denial of the last link, same 'will not' conclusion.
A chain, but the reasoning is flawed: it denies the first condition (no seminar) and concludes the result fails. Jun could earn extra credit some other way. The original is valid.

questions.stimulus: More than half of the engineers at Merrin Software work on the company's mobile app team, and more than half of Merrin's engineers voted in favor of the proposal, put forward by the company's founders, to switch to a four-day workweek. So a majority of the engineers on the mobile app team must have voted in favor of switching to a four-day workweek.

choices: overlooks the possibility that some of the company's engineers did not vote on the proposal at all
takes for granted that because most engineers favored the switch, the switch would benefit the company
relies on figures about the company as a whole to draw a conclusion about every engineer on the mobile app team
overlooks the possibility that none of the engineers on the mobile app team voted in favor of the switch
fails to consider that the engineers who did not vote for the switch could be concentrated on the mobile app team
questions.explanation: Two majorities of the same group must overlap, but only by a little: with 100 engineers, 51 on mobile and 51 in favor, all 49 non-supporters could be on mobile, leaving just 2 mobile supporters. (E) names exactly this. (D) is the trap: it describes something impossible, since two majorities of one group must share at least one member. The 49 who voted no could all be mobile engineers. We need an answer that says the opponents might be clustered on the mobile team.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The premise already says more than half of all engineers voted yes; non-voters don't change that.

CORRECT. Two majorities must overlap, but only a little. With 100 engineers, 51 on mobile and 51 in favor, all 49 non-supporters could sit on mobile, leaving just 2 mobile supporters out of 51.

passages.title: Constructed editions of unfinished novels
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
When a novelist dies leaving a book unfinished, her editors face a choice. Increasingly, they have resolved it by producing what might be called a constructed edition: a single continuous reading text assembled from the surviving drafts, with the editor choosing among competing versions of each scene and supplying bridges where the drafts break off. The practice has drawn sharp criticism from textual scholars, who argue that it misrepresents the very works it claims to rescue and that a responsible edition would print the drafts as drafts.

The critics’ favorite example is The Lantern Year, which Ilse Korvath left in three drafts when she died in 1961. The drafts disagree about the order of the last chapters and even about the fate of the narrator, yet the 1964 edition settles both questions in Korvath’s name: its title page announces a novel by Korvath, not a novel arranged by her editor. Worse, the edition hides its seams. Reviewers have praised its abrupt, splintered final chapter as Korvath’s boldest experiment, though that chapter was spliced together from fragments of two drafts written eleven years apart. And because teachers assign the 1964 text and translators work from it, scholars who return to the manuscripts find their alternative arrangements treated as curiosities. An editor’s provisional judgment, the critics conclude, has hardened into a permanent text.

These objections are serious, but they tell against careless constructed editions rather than against the practice itself. Even a novel its author saw through the press reflects choices made by others: editors who proposed cuts, copy editors who regularized punctuation, typesetters whose errors went uncorrected. No one concludes that such novels are not really their authors’ work. A constructed edition differs from them in degree, not in kind. What matters is not whether an editor intervenes but whether the intervention is disclosed.

Nor need a constructed edition conceal anything. When Tomas Ebbesen’s unfinished Salt Roads appeared in 1972, its editor printed an afterword that identified every passage she had moved or bridged and listed the principal variants she had set aside. Readers who wish to know where the author ends and the editor begins can find out; readers who wish simply to read the novel can do that too. The alternative the critics favor, an edition reproducing every cancelled line and marginal query, has real value, but almost no one except specialists reads such editions, and a novel that survives only in that form survives, for most readers, in name alone. Disclosure cannot entirely keep a well-made reading text from becoming the standard one, and editors should say plainly that their arrangements are provisional. But that is a reason to make constructed editions candidly, not a reason to stop making them.

passages.title: Adverse possession and the industry rationale
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Passage A

Under the law of Aldmere, a person who openly occupies another’s land without permission for an unbroken period of fifteen years acquires title to it, and the record owner’s claim is extinguished. The rule is often described as a concession to wrongdoers, an awkward exception to the principle that no one should profit from a trespass. That description misunderstands it.

Land is scarce, and land left idle benefits no one. The doctrine transfers title from owners who leave land unused to possessors who put it to work: who fence it, graze it, plant it, or build on it. The fifteen-year period is best understood not as a measure of the owner’s patience but as a measure of the possessor’s investment. A possessor who has worked land for that long has typically sunk labor and money into it that would be lost if she were ejected, while an owner who has ignored the land for fifteen years has shown how little it means to him.

This account explains a feature of the doctrine that otherwise looks puzzling: Aldmere courts do not ask whether the possessor believed the land was hers or knew that it was not. If the doctrine existed to protect honest mistakes, her state of mind would be decisive. Because it exists to reward productive use, her state of mind is beside the point; a knowing possessor who farms a neglected field contributes as much as a mistaken one.

Understood in this way, the doctrine needs no apology. It is the law’s means of ensuring that land does not lie fallow merely because the person holding title has lost interest in it.

Passage B

Defenders of adverse possession often present it as a reward for industry, a way of moving land from idle owners to productive possessors. The decisions of Aldmere’s courts fit this account poorly. Judges there have awarded title to possessors who did little more than fence a meadow and graze a few sheep on it, yet they denied title to a possessor who had tended an orchard on a neighbor’s hillside for sixteen years, because the orchard could not be seen from the public road. Visibility, not productivity, decided the case, as it often does.

The industry account also equates an owner’s nonuse with neglect. But some owners leave land unused deliberately, to let a woodland regenerate or to protect a watershed. Such restraint is an exercise of ownership, not a sign of indifference to it.

Most tellingly, Aldmere law suspends the fifteen-year period while the owner is a minor or is legally incapacitated, so that a possessor’s labor during those years counts for nothing. These rules make sense only if the doctrine is concerned with an owner’s failure to object to a possession that the owner could have noticed and challenged. A rule designed to reward labor would have no reason to discount labor performed while the owner happened to be a child.

passages.title: Maranho and the telegraph in the Torrin Valley
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
For most of the nineteenth century, the farming districts of the Torrin Valley suffered periodic subsistence crises. When a local harvest failed, grain prices in the affected district could triple within weeks, and deaths from hunger and associated disease rose sharply. After 1880 such crises became far less deadly, and historians long credited the change to hardier seed varieties introduced in the 1870s, which were thought to have made harvests less likely to fail in the first place.

In a 1994 study, the economic historian Rosa Maranho argued that this explanation overlooked a striking pattern. Harvest failures did not become notably rarer after 1880; what changed was their consequences, and the change came first to districts whose market towns had been connected to the telegraph.
