Before the telegraph, a merchant in a well-supplied district learned of a shortage elsewhere only when travelers brought the news, often after prices there had peaked. Once price reports could be sent in hours, merchants could ship grain toward a district as soon as its prices began to rise, keeping them from climbing to levels at which the poorest households could no longer buy food. As evidence, Maranho showed that the gap between grain prices in connected towns narrowed sharply after each town gained a telegraph office, while the gap among unconnected towns did not.

The thesis drew two objections. Some critics noted that many connected towns also acquired rail links in the same decade, and argued that cheaper transport, not faster news, accounted for the narrowing. Others doubted that merchants would behave as Maranho supposed, contending that traders who knew of a shortage might as readily withhold grain to drive prices higher. Maranho answered the first objection by pointing to six towns that had telegraph offices for at least seven years before any railway reached them; in each, the price gap narrowed when the telegraph arrived, not when the railway did. The second objection she could answer only by appeal to the price data themselves.

The discovery in 2009 of the business records of the Ostrup trading house, a grain firm with agents in eleven valley towns, allowed merchant conduct to be examined directly. The records show agents ordering shipments within two or three days of telegraphed reports of rising prices, and they contain no instance of the firm holding back stock in response to such a report. But they also reveal something Maranho had not anticipated: in towns where the firm’s agents could not obtain credit from a local bank, telegraphed reports of shortages elsewhere produced few shipments, and prices there behaved much as they had before the telegraph. Information, it appears, reduced the toll of harvest failures only where merchants had the means to act on it.

passages.title: Double couplets in Lake Tarnholm
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
In many lakes fed by glacial meltwater, sediment accumulates on the lake floor in annual bands called varves. Each summer, meltwater carries silt and sand into the lake, where the coarse particles settle quickly into a thicker, coarse layer; in winter, when ice seals the lake and inflow nearly stops, fine clay settles slowly into a thin, fine layer above it. Because each coarse-and-fine pair, or couplet, normally represents one year, geologists can date sediment at any depth by counting couplets down from the surface. Lake Tarnholm, in a glaciated mountain valley, seems to defy this method. Cores from its floor contain about 4,100 couplets above the gravel left when the valley’s ice retreated, yet radiocarbon dating of leaf fragments in the lowest sediment indicates that the lake is only about 2,050 years old.

Some researchers concluded that the radiocarbon dates must be in error. But the geologist Ines Haldor points out that the most common source of such error in lake sediment, carbon from ancient limestone dissolved in the water, makes samples appear older than they are, not younger, and in any case does not affect leaves, which take their carbon from the air. Haldor proposes instead that the couplet count is right but its interpretation is wrong. Tarnholm, she argues, receives two separate floods of sediment each year: one in late spring, when snow melts on the low slopes around the lake, and another in late summer, when the small glacier at the head of the valley reaches its peak melt. Between the two, inflow slackens for several weeks and fine clay settles, so each flood leaves its own couplet.

The strongest evidence for this view comes from a band of volcanic ash in the cores, chemically matched to an eruption of Mount Ossel that, according to regional monastery chronicles, occurred 1,140 years before the cores were taken. The ash lies beneath 2,276 couplets, close to the 2,280 that two per year would produce, and the 1,814 couplets below it span the 910 years between the lake’s formation and the eruption; a doubling that holds on both sides of the ash is hard to attribute to a single episode, such as a century of unusual floods. The couplets also differ as Haldor predicts. The low slopes around Tarnholm are underlain by dark slate and the glacier by pale, feldspar-rich granite, and in the cores couplets with granite-rich coarse layers alternate regularly with couplets whose coarse layers are mostly slate. At nearby Lake Vessel, in a valley without a glacier, couplet count and radiocarbon age agree within a few decades. Haldor’s account does not yet explain why a handful of intervals contain single rather than double couplets, though she suggests that these record years in which a cool summer kept the glacier from sending a distinct flood downstream.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Constructed editions of unfinished novels take no greater liberties with an author’s work than ordinary publishing does, so textual scholars’ objections to them are unfounded.
The history of the 1964 edition of The Lantern Year shows how an editor’s provisional arrangement of an unfinished novel can harden into a permanent text.
The objections critics raise against constructed editions of unfinished novels are reasons to prepare such editions openly, not reasons to abandon them.
Editions that reproduce an unfinished novel’s drafts in full serve only specialists and should therefore give way to constructed editions meant for general readers.
Because constructed editions present editors’ decisions as the author’s own, editors of unfinished novels should publish the surviving drafts as drafts.
questions.explanation: The passage lays out the critics’ case (paragraphs 1–2), replies that it tells against careless editions rather than the practice (paragraph 3), and ends that the remaining worry is ‘a reason to make constructed editions candidly, not a reason to stop making them’ (paragraph 4). That is C. A overstates the author, who says a constructed edition differs from ordinary publishing ‘in degree,’ so it does take greater liberties; B is the critics’ example, and E is the critics’ conclusion.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall point about constructed editions.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Whole passage, especially the first sentence of P3 and the last sentence of P4.

breakdown.analysis: Who wins the argument? The critics get two paragraphs, but the author answers them: their objections hit careless editions, not the practice (P3), and disclosure answers the hidden-seams worry (P4). The last sentence is the thesis in miniature. We need an answer that keeps both halves: the critics have a point, but the fix is candor, not abandonment.

choices.note: Too strong. The author says a constructed edition differs from ordinary publishing ‘in degree, not in kind,’ which concedes it does take more liberties. And she calls the objections ‘serious,’ not unfounded.
Tempting. This is the critics’ Lantern Year story from P2, told accurately. But it’s one example inside the critics’ case, and the author goes on to answer it.
CORRECT. This matches P3’s ‘they tell against careless constructed editions rather than against the practice itself’ and P4’s closing line: candor, not abandonment.
Half right, then too far. The author does say draft editions are read by almost no one but specialists, but she grants they have ‘real value’ and never says they should give way to anything.
Wrong party. This is the critics’ view from P1 (‘a responsible edition would print the drafts as drafts’). The author rejects it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the final chapter of the 1964 edition of The Lantern Year
choices: was praised by reviewers chiefly because it resolved the disagreements among Korvath’s three drafts
reflects the arrangement of the last chapters that Korvath preferred in her latest surviving draft
was later rearranged by scholars who returned to Korvath’s manuscripts and found an alternative ending
is the only portion of the novel for which more than one complete draft has survived
was assembled from fragments of two drafts that Korvath wrote more than a decade apart
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the abrupt final chapter ‘was spliced together from fragments of two drafts written eleven years apart,’ which is E. A gives reviewers the wrong reason (they praised it as a bold experiment), B and D are never stated, and C twists the passage: later scholars’ arrangements are treated as curiosities, not adopted.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage actually says about the final chapter of the 1964 edition.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P2, the fourth sentence (‘Reviewers have praised...’).

breakdown.analysis: This is a straight detail question, so go back and read the sentence. Reviewers praised the chapter as Korvath’s ‘boldest experiment,’ but it was ‘spliced together from fragments of two drafts written eleven years apart.’ We need a paraphrase of that.

choices.note: Wrong reason. Reviewers praised the chapter as a bold experiment, not as a fix for the drafts’ disagreements.
We don’t know this. The passage never says which arrangement Korvath preferred; the whole problem is that the drafts disagree.
Twisted. Later scholars propose alternative arrangements, but P2 says these are ‘treated as curiosities.’ Nothing says the edition’s chapter was rearranged.
Never stated. The passage says the drafts disagree about the last chapters, not that the final chapter is the only part with multiple drafts.
CORRECT. ‘Fragments of two drafts written eleven years apart’ = two drafts more than a decade apart.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward the practice of producing constructed editions of unfinished novels is most accurately described as
choices: reluctant tolerance
qualified approval
unreserved enthusiasm
detached neutrality
growing disillusionment
questions.explanation: The author defends constructed editions: the critics’ objections ‘tell against careless constructed editions rather than against the practice itself,’ and the conclusion is to keep making them ‘candidly.’ But she also grants that the objections are ‘serious’ and that disclosure ‘cannot entirely’ keep a reading text from becoming the standard one. Support with a reservation is qualified approval, B. A is the near miss, but the author argues for the practice rather than merely putting up with it; C ignores her concessions, and D and E do not fit an author who takes a side.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the author feels about constructed editions.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P3, first sentence; P4, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Is the author for or against? For: the objections hit careless editions, not the practice, and the last line says keep making them. But not blindly: she calls the objections ‘serious’ and admits disclosure can’t fully stop a reading text from hardening into the standard one. So: in favor, with a reservation.

choices.note: Tempting, because the author makes concessions. But ‘tolerance’ means putting up with something you’d rather not. The author actively argues for the practice and against the critics’ alternative.
CORRECT. Approval (keep making them; the objections don’t defeat the practice) plus qualification (they must be made candidly; disclosure can’t solve everything).
Too strong. The author calls the objections ‘serious’ and concedes a problem that disclosure can’t fully fix.
Wrong. The author takes a clear side against the critics.
No basis. Nothing suggests the author’s view sours over the passage; it ends on a defense of the practice.

questions.stem: In saying that a novel surviving only in an edition of its drafts survives “in name alone” (fourth paragraph), the author most likely means that such a novel
choices: would keep its title while losing most of the text that its author wrote
would be known about by most readers without actually being read by them
would be attributed to its author even though an editor had arranged it
would be studied by specialists chiefly for the variants that it records
would have no claim to be regarded as a finished work of literature
questions.explanation: The phrase follows the claim that ‘almost no one except specialists reads such editions,’ so a novel available only that way exists for most readers as a title they know of but do not read, which is B. A takes ‘name’ literally: nothing in a full draft edition is lost, since it reproduces every cancelled line. C describes the constructed edition, the opposite case, and E brings in a question of finished status the sentence does not raise.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain what ‘in name alone’ means in context.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P4, the fourth sentence (the one about draft editions read by ‘almost no one except specialists’).

breakdown.analysis: Read the whole sentence: draft editions have value, ‘but almost no one except specialists reads such editions,’ so the novel survives ‘for most readers, in name alone.’ Ask: what happens to most readers? They don’t read it. They may know it exists, but that’s all. We need ‘known of, not read.’

choices.note: Dictionary trap. ‘Name’ isn’t a literal title left behind after the text is lost. A full draft edition preserves everything, ‘every cancelled line and marginal query.’
CORRECT. The sentence ties the phrase to who reads such editions: most readers know the novel only as a name.
Reversed. Being arranged by an editor yet credited to the author describes the constructed edition, not the draft edition.
Partly true of specialists, but the phrase is about ‘most readers,’ not specialists, and the passage never says variants are what specialists study.
Different issue. The sentence is about readership, not whether the work counts as finished.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the 1964 edition of The Lantern Year?
choices: It should be withdrawn in favor of an edition that reproduces Korvath’s three drafts in full.
It took no greater liberties with Korvath’s drafts than a publisher ordinarily takes with a finished novel.
Its arrangement of the last chapters is more satisfying than any that later scholars have proposed.
It would have been less open to the critics’ objections had it disclosed where its editor intervened.
Its editor was justified in presenting the novel as Korvath’s because Korvath had left three drafts.
questions.explanation: The author says the critics’ objections tell against careless editions, that what matters is ‘whether the intervention is disclosed,’ and that an afterword like the one in Salt Roads lets readers see ‘where the author ends and the editor begins.’ The 1964 edition hid its seams, so disclosure would have answered at least that objection, which is D. B is the trap: the author says a constructed edition differs from ordinary publishing ‘in degree,’ which implies greater liberties. A contradicts her defense of the practice, and C and E are never suggested.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the author would say about the 1964 Korvath edition.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P2 (what the critics say the edition did), P3 (last sentence) and P4 (the afterword).

breakdown.analysis: The author never defends the 1964 edition by name. But she says the objections hit careless editions, and the 1964 edition’s sin in P2 was hiding its seams. P4’s afterword is the cure for that. So the author would say: if it had disclosed its changes, it would have been on firmer ground. We need something that modest.

choices.note: Opposite. The author argues against replacing reading texts with draft editions, which ‘almost no one except specialists reads.’
Tempting, because P3 compares constructed editions with ordinary publishing. But it says they differ ‘in degree, not in kind’: same sort of thing, more of it. That means more liberties, not none.
We don’t know this. The author never judges the quality of the arrangement or compares it with scholars’ alternatives.
CORRECT. P3 says disclosure is what matters, and P4 shows how an afterword answers the hidden-seams worry the 1964 edition invited.
Unsupported, and the reason is odd: leaving three disagreeing drafts is the problem, not a justification. The author’s defense rests on degree-not-kind and on disclosure.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the afterword printed in the 1972 edition of Salt Roads, as that afterword is described in the passage?
choices: a museum’s decision to display a damaged fresco in its damaged state rather than restore it
a label beside a restored fresco identifying which portions were repainted by the museum’s conservators
a conservator’s choice to repaint the missing portions of a fresco in a style matching the original
a catalog listing every fresco that scholars have attributed to a particular painter
an essay in which a scholar argues that a restored fresco should be returned to its damaged state
questions.explanation: The afterword accompanies a reading text and tells readers exactly where the editor moved or bridged material. The label does the same for a restored fresco: the restoration stays, and viewers are told which parts are not the original artist’s, which is B. C is the restoration itself, the analogue of the constructed edition rather than its afterword; A is the analogue of a draft edition, and E is the critics’ position.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the afterword’s role to a case from a different field.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P4, the second and third sentences (the afterword and what it lets readers do).

breakdown.analysis: Strip the afterword down: (1) a finished-looking version is presented; (2) a note alongside it identifies exactly which parts someone other than the creator supplied; (3) so the audience can enjoy the whole and still tell creator from editor. The right answer needs all three: a restored work plus disclosure of what was restored.

choices.note: This matches the critics’ alternative, printing the drafts as drafts: leave the damage and don’t restore. No disclosure of an intervention, because there’s no intervention.
CORRECT. Restoration stays (like the reading text), and the label marks the repainted parts (like the afterword’s list of moved and bridged passages).

Tempting, because it’s about the same fresco project. But repainting in matching style is the constructed edition itself, the intervention, not the note that discloses it. Done without a label, it’s the Lantern Year problem.
Out of scope. A catalog of attributions doesn’t separate one creator’s work from another’s within a single piece.
This is the critics’ argument against reconstruction transposed to frescoes, not the afterword.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: the conditions under which the courts of Aldmere have denied title to possessors of land
whether the adverse possession doctrine of Aldmere ought to be reformed or abolished
the historical origins of the rule that a possessor may acquire title after fifteen years
the protection that Aldmere law extends to owners who are minors or legally incapacitated
the purpose that best explains a rule allowing possessors to acquire title to another’s land
questions.explanation: Passage A argues that the adverse possession rule exists to reward productive use; passage B argues that its features show it is concerned instead with an owner’s failure to object. Both are about what purpose the rule serves, which is E. Choices A and D are topics only passage B raises, and neither passage proposes reform (B) or traces history (C).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the topic that both passages are mainly about.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, P2–P4; passage B, all three paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A says the rule is a reward for industry. Passage B says the courts’ decisions and the minority exception show it’s really about the owner failing to object. Different answers, same question: why does this rule exist? A ‘both’ answer has to fit both passages, not just one.

choices.note: Only passage B. The orchard case appears only in B, and A never discusses when title is denied.
Neither passage. Passage A says the doctrine ‘needs no apology’; passage B explains the doctrine differently but never asks for reform.
Neither passage gives any history of the rule.
Only passage B, and even there the minority exception is evidence about the rule’s purpose, not the main topic.
CORRECT. Passage A: the purpose is rewarding productive use. Passage B: the features point to an owner’s failure to object. Same question, different answers.

questions.stem: According to passage A, the courts of Aldmere, in deciding whether a possessor has acquired title, do not consider
choices: whether the possessor believed that the land was her own
whether the possessor’s occupation could be seen from a public road
whether the owner had given the possessor permission to occupy the land
how much the possessor has invested in the land during the occupation
how long the possessor has occupied the land without interruption
questions.explanation: Passage A’s third paragraph says Aldmere courts ‘do not ask whether the possessor believed the land was hers or knew that it was not,’ which is A. B is the trap: visibility comes from passage B, which says it often decides cases. C and E are part of the rule itself in passage A’s first sentence (occupation ‘without permission’ for ‘an unbroken period’), and passage A never says courts ignore investment (D).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage A says the courts leave out of the decision.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, P3, first sentence; P1 for the elements of the rule.

breakdown.analysis: Go to passage A’s third paragraph: the courts ‘do not ask whether the possessor believed the land was hers.’ That’s the answer. Watch for elements that the rule does require (permission, time) and for anything borrowed from passage B.

choices.note: CORRECT. Passage A, P3: courts don’t ask about the possessor’s belief, which A says is ‘beside the point.’
Wrong passage. Visibility is passage B’s point, and B says it often decides cases, the opposite of ‘not considered.’
Part of the rule. Passage A’s first sentence requires occupation ‘without permission,’ so permission matters.
Not stated. Passage A treats the fifteen-year period as a measure of investment but never says courts disregard it.
Part of the rule. Passage A requires ‘an unbroken period of fifteen years.’

questions.stem: The authors of the passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: a person who openly occupies another’s land for fifteen years can acquire title to it under Aldmere law
a possessor who knows that the land is not hers can acquire title under the law of Aldmere
the courts of Aldmere have denied title to a possessor whose orchard could not be seen from a public road
the fifteen-year period is best understood as measuring a possessor’s investment in the land
the rule suspending the fifteen-year period for owners who are minors should be abolished
questions.explanation: Passage A says outright that the fifteen-year period is ‘a measure of the possessor’s investment.’ Passage B argues that suspending the period for minors makes sense only if the doctrine concerns the owner’s failure to object, and that a rule designed to reward labor would not discount labor done in those years, so passage B rejects that reading. That is D. Choice A states a rule both accept, B and C are points only one passage addresses, and E is raised by neither.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim one author would affirm and the other would deny.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, P2 (third sentence); passage B, P3.

breakdown.analysis: For a disagree question, both authors must take a side. Passage A: the period measures ‘the possessor’s investment.’ Passage B: the period is suspended for minors whatever the possessor invests, so the doctrine must be about the owner’s failure to object. That’s a direct clash over what the period measures.

choices.note: Both agree. Passage A states this rule, and passage B discusses it without disputing it.
Only passage A takes a side: it says a knowing possessor can acquire title, while passage B never discusses the possessor’s state of mind.
Only B. The orchard case appears only in passage B, and A says nothing about it.
CORRECT. Passage A affirms it in so many words; passage B’s minority argument denies that the doctrine is built to reward the possessor’s labor.
Neither. Passage B uses the suspension as evidence and passage A never mentions it; nobody proposes abolishing it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A describes a legal doctrine and the debate surrounding it without taking sides; passage B criticizes the doctrine on the basis of several court decisions.
Passage A defends a legal doctrine by attributing a purpose to it; passage B argues that no purpose could justify the doctrine as the courts have applied it.
Passage A defends a legal doctrine by attributing a purpose to it; passage B argues that the doctrine’s features point to a different purpose.
Passage A proposes reforming a legal doctrine; passage B argues that the proposed reform conflicts with features of the doctrine that are well settled.
Both passages defend a legal doctrine, but passage B relies on court decisions that passage A overlooks or misdescribes.
questions.explanation: Passage A defends adverse possession as a reward for productive use. Passage B does not attack the doctrine; it argues that the visibility cases and the minority exception show the doctrine is concerned with an owner’s failure to object, a different purpose. That is C. B is the near miss: passage B never says the doctrine is unjustifiable. Choice A misdescribes passage A, which takes a side, and D invents a reform.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how passage B relates to passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, P1 and P4 (its stance); passage B, P1 and P3 (its stance).

breakdown.analysis: Is passage B against the doctrine, or against passage A’s explanation of it? Read B’s last paragraph: the rules ‘make sense only if the doctrine is concerned with an owner’s failure to object.’ That’s an alternative purpose, not a rejection of the doctrine. So: A defends by purpose X; B says the features fit purpose Y.

choices.note: Wrong about passage A, which takes a clear side: the doctrine ‘needs no apology.’ And passage B criticizes passage A’s explanation, not the doctrine.
Tempting, because passage B is critical. But passage B offers a purpose that does fit the doctrine’s features (‘make sense only if...’). It never says no purpose could justify the doctrine.
CORRECT. Passage A: industry. Passage B: the doctrine’s features (visibility, the suspension for minors) point to the owner’s failure to object.
Invented frame. Neither passage proposes a reform.
Half wrong. Passage A defends the doctrine; passage B doesn’t defend or attack it so much as reinterpret it. And passage B never says passage A misdescribes any court decision.

questions.stem: The author of passage A mentions that Aldmere courts do not ask about the possessor’s state of mind (first sentence of the third paragraph of passage A) primarily in order to
choices: concede a feature of the doctrine that the author’s own account of its purpose cannot readily explain
point to a feature of the doctrine that the author’s account of its purpose can explain
argue that the courts should begin to consider whether possessors acted in good faith
show that the doctrine was originally intended to protect possessors who made honest mistakes
distinguish the doctrine of Aldmere from rules elsewhere that reward a possessor’s good faith
questions.explanation: The sentence opens ‘This account explains a feature of the doctrine that otherwise looks puzzling,’ and the paragraph shows why the industry account makes the possessor’s state of mind irrelevant. The feature is offered as support for passage A’s account, which is B. Choice A reverses its role, C proposes a change passage A never proposes, D is the hypothesis passage A rejects (‘If the doctrine existed to protect honest mistakes...’), and E invents other jurisdictions.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why passage A brings up the courts’ indifference to the possessor’s state of mind.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, P3 (all three sentences).

breakdown.analysis: The paragraph’s first words give it away: ‘This account explains a feature of the doctrine that otherwise looks puzzling.’ The author is scoring a point: my theory explains something that would otherwise be strange. So the feature is evidence for passage A’s account.

choices.note: Reversed. Passage A says its account explains the feature; it isn’t conceding a problem.
CORRECT. ‘This account explains a feature of the doctrine that otherwise looks puzzling.’ The feature is offered as evidence for the industry account.
Opposite. Passage A says the possessor’s state of mind is properly ‘beside the point.’
Tempting, because the honest-mistakes idea appears in the paragraph. But it appears as a rejected alternative (‘If the doctrine existed to protect honest mistakes...’), not as history.
Out of scope. Passage A never mentions other jurisdictions.

questions.stem: The author of passage B would most likely respond to the claim in passage A that an owner who has ignored land for fifteen years “has shown how little it means to him” by pointing out that
choices: an owner may leave land unused for reasons that reflect concern for it rather than indifference
possessors who merely fence and graze land invest less in it than possessors who plant orchards
owners who cannot afford to develop their land should not lose title to it on that account
a possessor who has worked land for fifteen years would lose her investment if she were ejected
courts rarely inquire into how much an owner values land that he has chosen to leave unused
questions.explanation: Passage B’s second paragraph says the industry account ‘equates an owner’s nonuse with neglect,’ though some owners leave land unused ‘to let a woodland regenerate or to protect a watershed,’ which is ‘not a sign of indifference.’ That answers passage A’s claim directly, which is A. B is the trap: it comes from passage B’s orchard example, but that example targets the industry account generally, not the inference from nonuse to indifference. C invents an affordability point, and D is passage A’s own argument.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Predict passage B’s reply to one specific claim in passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, P2 (last sentence); passage B, P2.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A treats fifteen years of nonuse as proof the owner doesn’t care. Passage B has a paragraph aimed squarely at that move: nonuse isn’t neglect, because some owners hold off on purpose (regeneration, a watershed). So B would say: unused doesn’t mean unloved.

choices.note: CORRECT. Passage B, P2: deliberate restraint ‘is an exercise of ownership, not a sign of indifference to it.’
Tempting, because it’s drawn from passage B. But the orchard case answers ‘the doctrine rewards industry,’ not ‘nonuse shows the owner doesn’t care.’ It’s a real B point aimed at a different A claim.
We don’t know this. Passage B’s examples are deliberate choices (regeneration, a watershed), not owners who can’t afford development.
Wrong side. This is passage A’s own argument about the possessor’s sunk labor and money.
Never stated in passage B, and it wouldn’t rebut passage A’s claim even if true.

questions.stem: Passage B raises each of the following as a difficulty for the view that adverse possession rewards industry EXCEPT:
choices: the award of title to possessors whose use of the land was slight
the denial of title to a possessor whose occupation could not be seen from a public road
the existence of owners who leave land unused for purposes they consider worthwhile
the suspension of the fifteen-year period while the owner is a minor or is incapacitated
the doctrine’s indifference to whether the possessor believed the land to be her own
questions.explanation: The possessor’s state of mind appears only in passage A, which cites the courts’ indifference to it as support for the industry account; passage B never mentions it, so E is the exception. A and B come from passage B’s first paragraph (the meadow and the orchard), C from its second, and D from its third.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Four answers are difficulties passage B raises for the industry view. Find the one it doesn’t raise.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, all three paragraphs; passage A, P3 for the odd one out.

breakdown.analysis: List passage B’s difficulties: (1) title for slight use (fencing and grazing); (2) no title for an unseen orchard; (3) owners who leave land unused on purpose; (4) the suspension for minors and incapacitated owners. Anything else is the answer. Careful: the answer may appear in passage A, just not as a difficulty raised by passage B.

choices.note: Raised. Passage B, P1: title for possessors who ‘did little more than fence a meadow and graze a few sheep.’
Raised. Passage B, P1: the orchard grower lost ‘because the orchard could not be seen from the public road.’
Raised. Passage B, P2: owners who leave land unused to let a woodland regenerate or protect a watershed.
Raised. Passage B, P3: labor during the owner’s minority or incapacity ‘counts for nothing.’
CORRECT. This comes from passage A, P3, where it supports the industry view. Passage B never mentions the possessor’s state of mind.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the position taken in passage B relative to that taken in passage A?
choices: Possessors who acquire title under the doctrine generally go on to make more productive use of the land than its former owners did.
Fencing a meadow and grazing sheep on it require considerable labor and expense in the steep hill districts of Aldmere.
Courts in several neighboring jurisdictions consider whether a possessor acted in good faith when deciding disputes over title.
Aldmere courts have granted title to possessors who never worked the land but whose occupation the owner could easily have seen.
Some possessors in Aldmere have occupied land for fifteen years while sincerely believing that it was their own.
questions.explanation: Passage A says the doctrine rewards productive use; passage B says it turns on an owner’s failure to object to a possession the owner could have noticed. A grant of title with no productive use at all, where the owner could easily have seen the occupation, fits passage B’s account and is hard for passage A’s to explain, which is D. B is the trap: it would make fencing and grazing look industrious and so weaken one of passage B’s points. Choice A supports passage A, C concerns other jurisdictions, and E fits both accounts.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that favors passage B’s account of the doctrine over passage A’s.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, P2–P3 (industry); passage B, P1 and P3 (visibility and failure to object).

breakdown.analysis: What would separate the two theories? A case where they predict different outcomes. Industry theory: no work, no title. Failure-to-object theory: if the owner could see it and did nothing, title passes, work or no work. So we want title granted for a visible occupation with no productive use at all.

choices.note: Supports passage A, not passage B. If possessors really do put land to better use, the industry account looks better.

Tempting, because it’s about the meadow example. But it cuts the wrong way: if fencing and grazing take real labor, passage B’s claim that those possessors ‘did little more’ loses force, and the industry account looks better.
Irrelevant. Other jurisdictions’ rules say nothing about what Aldmere’s doctrine is for.
CORRECT. Title with zero industry but full visibility is exactly what passage B’s account predicts and passage A’s can’t explain.
Inert. Both accounts allow possessors who believed the land was theirs to gain title; this doesn’t favor either side.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Contrary to the long-held view, hardier seed varieties played no part in reducing the deadliness of harvest failures in the Torrin Valley after 1880.
Later evidence has largely confirmed Maranho’s thesis that faster price information made harvest failures less deadly, while showing that the effect depended on merchants’ credit.
The narrowing of grain price gaps among Torrin Valley towns after 1880 is better explained by the arrival of railways than by the spread of the telegraph.
The records of the Ostrup trading house demonstrate that grain merchants throughout the Torrin Valley did not withhold stock to drive up prices during shortages.
Access to bank credit, rather than access to price information, was what reduced the toll of subsistence crises in the Torrin Valley after 1880.
questions.explanation: The passage moves from the old seed explanation to Maranho’s telegraph thesis, through two objections, to the Ostrup records, which bear out her account of merchant behavior but show that information mattered only where merchants had credit. That is B. E is the trap: the last sentence makes credit a condition for information to work, not a replacement for it. A overstates the passage’s treatment of seeds, C is the critics’ view that Maranho rebutted, and D generalizes from one firm to all merchants.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the passage’s overall point.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Whole passage, especially P2 (the thesis) and the last sentence of P4.

breakdown.analysis: Track the story: old view (seeds) → Maranho (telegraph, faster price news) → objections → new records that back her on merchant behavior but add a condition (credit). The main point has to include Maranho’s thesis, its confirmation, and the credit twist, without letting the twist swallow the thesis.

choices.note: Too strong. The passage says harvest failures didn’t become rarer, which undercuts the seed explanation, but it never says seeds played ‘no part.’
CORRECT. Thesis (faster price information), confirmation (the Ostrup records on merchant conduct), and the qualification (credit), all in one sentence.
Wrong side. This is the first objection, which Maranho answered with the six towns.
Overgeneralized, and only a detail. The records show one firm never withheld stock; they say nothing about all merchants throughout the valley.

Tempting, because it picks up the last sentence. But that sentence says information reduced the toll ‘only where merchants had the means to act on it.’ Credit is a condition for information to work, not a rival cause.

questions.stem: The information in the passage most helps to answer which one of the following questions?
choices: Before the telegraph, how did merchants in well-supplied districts usually learn of shortages elsewhere?
By how much did deaths from hunger in the Torrin Valley decline in the decades after 1880?
Which towns in the Torrin Valley were the first to acquire rail links, and in what years?
Why were agents of the Ostrup trading house unable to obtain bank credit in some valley towns?
Did the seed varieties introduced in the 1870s raise average yields in districts lacking telegraph offices?
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says that before the telegraph a merchant learned of a shortage elsewhere ‘only when travelers brought the news,’ which answers A. D is the trap: the passage says some agents could not obtain credit but never says why. It gives no figures on deaths (B), names no rail towns or dates (C), and says nothing about yields by district (E).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the question the passage actually answers.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P2, the third sentence (‘Before the telegraph...’).

breakdown.analysis: Test each question against the text. The answerable one has its answer sitting in a sentence. Watch for questions on topics the passage mentions but doesn’t explain: mentioning a fact isn’t answering ‘why’ or ‘how much.’

choices.note: CORRECT. P2: a merchant learned of a shortage ‘only when travelers brought the news.’
No figures. P1 says crises became ‘far less deadly’ but gives no numbers.
Not named. P3 mentions rail links in the same decade and six towns that got the telegraph first, but names no towns and gives no years.
Tempting, because P4 does say some agents ‘could not obtain credit from a local bank.’ But the passage never says why.
Never addressed. The passage says nothing about yields, let alone by district.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following statements about the explanation that historians long gave for the declining deadliness of subsistence crises in the Torrin Valley?
choices: It presupposed that the decline came about chiefly through a reduction in how often harvests failed.
It attributed the decline chiefly to improvements in the speed and cost of transporting grain.
It was contradicted by the Ostrup records, which show that harvests failed as often after 1880 as before.
It was abandoned by most historians soon after Maranho’s study first appeared in 1994.
It could not account for the fact that grain prices in unconnected towns diverged after 1880.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the hardier seeds ‘were thought to have made harvests less likely to fail in the first place,’ so the old explanation depended on failures becoming rarer, which is A. C is the trap: it was Maranho’s study, not the Ostrup records, that showed failures did not become rarer. B describes the railway objection, D is never stated, and E distorts the data, which show only that the gap among unconnected towns did not narrow.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what can be inferred about the old seed explanation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P1 (last sentence); P2 (first two sentences).

breakdown.analysis: What did the seed story need to be true? Seeds work by making harvests ‘less likely to fail in the first place.’ So it needs failures to have become rarer. That’s exactly what Maranho denies in P2. We want an answer about that built-in assumption.

choices.note: CORRECT. P1: the seeds ‘were thought to have made harvests less likely to fail in the first place.’ The explanation rides on fewer failures.
Wrong explanation. Transport is the critics’ alternative in P3, not the historians’ seed story.
Tempting, because the claim about failures is real. But it’s Maranho’s 1994 study that says failures ‘did not become notably rarer.’ The Ostrup records concern merchants’ conduct.
We don’t know this. The passage never says how historians responded to Maranho.
Distorted. P2 says the gap among unconnected towns ‘did not’ narrow, not that their prices diverged; and nothing says the seed story was tested against this.

questions.stem: The passage mentions six towns that had telegraph offices for at least seven years before any railway reached them (fourth sentence of the third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that the telegraph spread through the Torrin Valley more quickly than the railways did
suggest that rail links did little to lower the cost of moving grain between valley towns
identify the towns in which the Ostrup trading house later established its agents
illustrate how merchants responded when they learned of shortages in distant districts
show how the effects of two developments that often coincided could be told apart
questions.explanation: Critics said rail links, which arrived in the same decade as the telegraph, explained the narrowing price gaps. In the six towns the two arrived years apart, so Maranho could see which one the narrowing followed, which is E. B is the trap: the example shows the narrowing came with the telegraph, not that railways failed to cut transport costs. A overgeneralizes from six towns, C links them to the Ostrup firm without basis, and D describes the second objection’s subject.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what work the six-town example does.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P3, sentences 2 and 4 (the railway objection and Maranho’s answer).

breakdown.analysis: Why pick towns where the telegraph came seven years before the railway? Because elsewhere the two came together, so you couldn’t tell which one did the work. Pull them apart in time and see which arrival lines up with the narrowing. That’s a way of separating two causes.

choices.note: Overgeneralized. Six towns got the telegraph first; that says nothing about the valley as a whole.
Tempting, because the example weakens the railway objection. But it shows the narrowing came with the telegraph; it doesn’t show railways failed to cut costs.
No link. The passage never connects the six towns to the Ostrup firm’s eleven towns.
Wrong objection. Merchant behavior is the second objection, which Maranho could answer only with the price data.
CORRECT. Two developments that came together in most towns came years apart in these six, so their effects could be distinguished.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen Maranho’s response to the objection that cheaper transport accounted for the narrowing of price gaps?
choices: In towns that acquired rail links before telegraph offices, price gaps with other towns narrowed when the railway arrived.
Agents of grain firms throughout the Torrin Valley commonly ordered shipments within a few days of receiving telegraphed reports of rising prices.
In the six towns, neither the routes nor the charges for carrying grain changed between the telegraph’s arrival and the railway’s.
The six towns were among the largest and most prosperous market towns in the Torrin Valley throughout the period.
Deaths from hunger in the six towns declined still further in the years after the railways finally reached them.
questions.explanation: Maranho’s response is that in six towns the price gap narrowed when the telegraph arrived, years before the railway. A defender of the transport objection could still say some other transport improvement, such as new roads or lower carrying charges, came at the same time as the telegraph. C rules that out. B is the trap: it supports Maranho on the second objection, about merchant behavior, not on transport. A, if anything, helps the critics.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that makes Maranho’s six-town reply to the transport objection stronger.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P3, sentences 2 and 4.

breakdown.analysis: Maranho’s reply: in six towns, the gap narrowed with the telegraph, not the railway. The leftover hole: maybe transport got cheaper some other way at the same time. So ask, how could the critic still win? We want an answer that shuts that door: transport didn’t change when the telegraph came.

choices.note: Helps the critics. If rail alone narrowed gaps elsewhere, cheaper transport looks like a real cause.
Tempting, because it supports Maranho in general. But it answers the second objection (would merchants ship?), not the first (was it transport rather than news?).
CORRECT. With routes and charges unchanged when the telegraph came, cheaper transport can’t explain the narrowing in those towns.
Irrelevant to the timing argument. Size doesn’t tell us what caused the narrowing.
Doesn’t help. A later fall in deaths after rail arrived, if anything, suggests rail mattered too.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information in the passage?
choices: The Ostrup trading house had agents in each of the six towns that acquired telegraph offices before rail links.
Until the Ostrup records were found, the evidence that merchants did not commonly withhold grain during shortages was indirect.
The Ostrup records indicate that Maranho’s price data overstated how much price gaps narrowed after the telegraph arrived.
Merchants in towns where bank credit was unavailable deliberately withheld grain when prices elsewhere began to rise.
Once railways reached the valley’s towns, telegraphed price reports ceased to have any effect on merchants’ shipments.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says Maranho could answer the withholding objection ‘only by appeal to the price data themselves,’ and the fourth says the Ostrup records first allowed merchant conduct ‘to be examined directly.’ So the earlier evidence was indirect, which is B. D is the trap: few shipments where credit was lacking points to inability to act, not deliberate withholding. Nothing supports A, C, or E.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the passage supports best.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P3 (last sentence) and P4 (first sentence).

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase. Combine statements and watch for answers that turn ‘few shipments’ into a motive, or that link facts the passage never connects. Here two sentences fit together: Maranho’s only answer to withholding was the price data, and the Ostrup records were the first direct look at conduct.

choices.note: Unsupported link. The passage never says where the firm’s eleven towns were relative to the six.
CORRECT. ‘Only by appeal to the price data’ plus ‘allowed merchant conduct to be examined directly’ means earlier evidence was indirect.
Never stated. The records bear out her account of merchant behavior; nothing says her price data were overstated.

Tempting, because P4 says shipments were few where agents lacked credit. But that shows they couldn’t act, not that they chose to withhold. The records show ‘no instance’ of the firm holding back stock.
Too strong and unsupported. The passage never says railways ended the telegraph’s effect.

questions.stem: Which one of the following studies would be most useful in evaluating the claim made in the last sentence of the passage?
choices: a comparison of deaths from hunger during harvest failures in districts connected to the telegraph and in unconnected districts, both before and after 1880
a study of whether grain firms other than the Ostrup trading house also refrained from withholding stock when prices rose
a comparison of the change in hunger deaths after the telegraph’s arrival between districts where merchants could obtain credit and districts where they could not
a measurement of how much the price gap between towns with banks lending to grain merchants narrowed after those towns acquired telegraph offices
a survey of the interest rates that banks in the Torrin Valley charged to grain merchants in the decades after 1880
questions.explanation: The last sentence says information reduced the toll of harvest failures ‘only where merchants had the means to act on it.’ Testing that requires comparing the telegraph’s effect on deaths where merchants had credit with its effect where they did not, which is C. D is the trap: it studies only towns with credit and measures prices rather than deaths, so with no comparison group it cannot show the effect was limited to such towns. A tests whether information mattered at all, not whether credit conditioned it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the study that would best test the passage’s final claim.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P4, last sentence (and the credit finding just before it).

breakdown.analysis: The claim has two parts: information reduced the toll, and only where merchants could act (credit). An ‘only where’ claim needs a comparison: with credit vs. without. And it’s about the toll (deaths), so the study should measure deaths, or at least compare both groups. We need a with-vs-without-credit comparison after the telegraph arrived.

choices.note: Tempting, because it’s a careful comparison. But it tests whether the telegraph mattered at all, not whether its effect depended on credit.
Wrong question. Withholding by other firms bears on the second objection, not on the credit condition.
CORRECT. It compares the telegraph’s effect on deaths in places with and without merchant credit, exactly what ‘only where merchants had the means’ requires.
Tempting, because it mentions both banks and the telegraph. But it looks only at towns with credit, so there’s nothing to compare against, and it measures prices instead of the toll.
Irrelevant detail. Interest rates don’t show whether the telegraph’s effect depended on credit.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Haldor’s hypothesis that the lake receives two floods of sediment a year plausibly reconciles Lake Tarnholm’s couplet count with its radiocarbon age.
The radiocarbon dates for Lake Tarnholm’s sediment must be mistaken, since the count of couplets in its cores shows that the lake is about 4,100 years old.
Counting couplets is an unreliable method of dating lake sediment, as the conflicting evidence from Lake Tarnholm and nearby Lake Vessel demonstrates.
Ash from an eruption of Mount Ossel provides a more reliable means of dating the sediment of lakes in Lake Tarnholm’s region than radiocarbon dating does.
Lake Tarnholm’s sediment contains two kinds of couplets, one derived from slate and the other from granite, because its catchment includes two types of bedrock.
questions.explanation: The passage sets out the conflict between about 4,100 couplets and a 2,050-year radiocarbon age, presents Haldor’s two-floods-a-year explanation, and gives the ash and bedrock evidence for it while noting one gap, which is A. B is the view Haldor rejects. C overgeneralizes, since Lake Vessel shows the method working where there is one flood a year, and D and E are supporting details.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the passage’s overall point.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Whole passage: P1 (the puzzle), P2 (the hypothesis), P3 (the evidence).

breakdown.analysis: Puzzle (twice as many couplets as years) → Haldor’s fix (two floods, two couplets a year) → evidence (ash, bedrock, Lake Vessel) with one loose end. The main point is the fix, with an appropriately hedged endorsement.

choices.note: CORRECT. The hypothesis and what it does (reconciles the count with the age); ‘plausibly’ fits the author’s hedge about the unexplained single couplets.
Wrong side. This is what ‘some researchers’ concluded, and Haldor rejects it in P2.
Too broad. At Lake Vessel the count and radiocarbon age agree, so the method works where there’s one flood a year.
Detail, distorted. The ash supports Haldor’s reading; the passage never ranks ash over radiocarbon for dating the region’s lakes.
Supporting detail. The slate/granite alternation is one piece of evidence in P3, not the main point.

questions.stem: In saying that the couplet count is right “but its interpretation is wrong” (third sentence of the second paragraph), Haldor most likely means that
choices: some couplets in the cores were overlooked because they were too thin to be distinguished from their neighbors
the radiocarbon ages have been taken to date the lake as a whole when they in fact date only the leaves
the couplets in the Tarnholm cores were formed by processes other than the melting of snow and glacial ice
geologists have wrongly assumed that couplets can be used to date the sediment of any lake fed by meltwater
the cores do contain about 4,100 couplets, but the lake did not take 4,100 years to deposit them
questions.explanation: The ‘interpretation’ is the standard reading from the first paragraph, that each couplet represents one year. Haldor accepts the count of about 4,100 but argues that two couplets form each year, so they took about 2,050 years to accumulate, which is E. A contradicts ‘the couplet count is right,’ B shifts the error to the radiocarbon dates, which she defends, C contradicts her two meltwater floods, and D overgeneralizes beyond Tarnholm.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain what Haldor means by ‘right’ count but ‘wrong’ interpretation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P2, third and fourth sentences; P1, third sentence (one couplet per year).

breakdown.analysis: Two parts. ‘Right’: the number, about 4,100, is accurate. ‘Interpretation’: what the number means, which P1 says is normally one couplet per year. So she’s saying: the count is fine, but at Tarnholm 4,100 couplets doesn’t mean 4,100 years.

choices.note: Contradicts ‘the couplet count is right.’ If couplets were overlooked, the count would be wrong.
Wrong target. Haldor defends the radiocarbon dates; her quarrel is with how the couplets are read.
Contradicts her theory. Both floods are meltwater, snow in spring and the glacier in late summer.
Too broad. She says one-per-year fails at Tarnholm, and Lake Vessel shows it works elsewhere.
CORRECT. The count is accurate; the one-couplet-per-year reading is what fails, so 4,100 couplets aren’t 4,100 years.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the most common source of radiocarbon error in lake sediment
choices: affects leaf fragments more strongly than it affects other kinds of organic material in the sediment
accounts for the discrepancy between the Tarnholm couplet count and the lake’s radiocarbon age
results from carbon that volcanic eruptions such as that of Mount Ossel release into lakes
tends to make the samples it affects appear older than they actually are
has been shown by Haldor to be absent from the water of Lake Tarnholm
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says this error, caused by carbon from ancient limestone, ‘makes samples appear older than they are, not younger,’ which is D. B is the trap: the error runs the wrong way to explain why the radiocarbon age is younger than the couplet count suggests. A reverses the passage, which says leaves are unaffected; C swaps limestone for volcanoes; and E is never stated.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the most common radiocarbon error.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P2, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Straight detail. The error comes from ancient limestone carbon, makes samples look older, and doesn’t touch leaves. Find the paraphrase.

choices.note: Reversed. Leaves ‘take their carbon from the air,’ so this error doesn’t affect them at all.
Tempting, but it runs the wrong way. An error that makes samples look older can’t explain a radiocarbon age that is younger than the couplet count suggests. That’s Haldor’s point.
Wrong source. The error comes from ‘ancient limestone dissolved in the water,’ not volcanoes.
CORRECT. ‘Makes samples appear older than they are, not younger.’
Never stated. Haldor says the error doesn’t affect leaves, not that it’s absent from the lake.

questions.stem: The author mentions Lake Vessel (second-to-last sentence of the passage) primarily in order to
choices: show that radiocarbon dating is more reliable than couplet counting in valleys that contain glaciers
illustrate how carbon from ancient limestone can distort the radiocarbon ages of lake sediment
suggest that ash from the eruption of Mount Ossel did not reach lakes outside the Tarnholm valley
offer a comparison case that lacks the feature Haldor holds responsible for Tarnholm’s double couplets
explain why a handful of intervals in the Tarnholm cores contain single rather than double couplets
questions.explanation: Lake Vessel lies in a valley without a glacier, and there couplet count and radiocarbon age agree. Since Haldor attributes Tarnholm’s second couplet each year to its glacier, Vessel is a control case that lacks that feature and shows the expected one-to-one result, which is D. A is the trap: Vessel shows the two methods agreeing, not one beating the other, and it has no glacier. E is the next sentence’s topic, and B and C are not discussed in connection with Vessel.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings up Lake Vessel.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P3, the second-to-last sentence; P2 for the role of the glacier.

breakdown.analysis: Why mention a lake with no glacier? Because Haldor says the glacier causes Tarnholm’s second flood. A nearby lake without one should show one couplet a year, and it does: count and radiocarbon agree. That’s a control: take away the cause, and the effect disappears.

choices.note: Tempting, because radiocarbon and couplets are both involved. But at Vessel they agree, so neither beats the other, and Vessel’s valley has no glacier.
Wrong topic. The limestone error comes up in P2 and has nothing to do with Vessel.
Never discussed. The passage says nothing about ash at Lake Vessel.
CORRECT. No glacier, no second flood, and the count matches the radiocarbon age: a comparison case lacking the proposed cause.
Wrong sentence. The single couplets are the subject of the last sentence, and Haldor’s suggestion there involves cool summers, not Vessel.

questions.stem: If Haldor’s suggestion about the intervals that contain single rather than double couplets (last sentence of the passage) is correct, which one of the following would most likely be true of the couplets in those intervals?
choices: Their coarse layers would consist mostly of particles of feldspar-rich granite.
They would be noticeably thicker than the couplets found in the rest of the cores.
They would contain traces of ash from eruptions earlier than that of Mount Ossel.
They would have formed in years when little snow fell on the slopes around the lake.
Their coarse layers would consist mostly of fragments of the dark slate.
questions.explanation: Haldor suggests that in those years a cool summer kept the glacier from sending its flood, so only the spring snowmelt from the low slopes reached the lake. The third paragraph says those slopes are underlain by dark slate, while the glacier sits on feldspar-rich granite, so the single couplets should be slate-rich, which is E. A reverses the two sources and is the main trap. D blames the wrong season’s melt, and B and C have no basis in the passage.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply Haldor’s suggestion to predict what the single couplets look like.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P3, last sentence (the suggestion) and the slate/granite sentence; P2 for which flood comes from where.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it: cool summer → no glacier flood → only the spring snowmelt flood that year. Spring flood comes off the low slopes → low slopes are dark slate. So the lone coarse layer should be slate, not granite.

choices.note: Reversed. Granite comes from beneath the glacier, and the glacier flood is the one that’s missing.
Unsupported. Nothing in the passage tells us how thick single couplets would be.
No basis. The passage mentions only the Ossel ash in the cores.
Wrong season. Haldor blames a cool summer that kept the glacier from melting, not a lack of snow on the slopes; the spring flood still comes.
CORRECT. The surviving flood is the spring snowmelt from the low slopes, which are underlain by dark slate.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question Haldor’s hypothesis?
choices: In some lakes far from Lake Tarnholm, couplets are known to form at a rate of more than one per year for reasons unrelated to glaciers.
The monastery chronicles that record the eruption of Mount Ossel also mention several earlier eruptions whose ash has not been found in the Tarnholm cores.
The glacier at the head of Tarnholm’s valley formed only about 600 years ago, after centuries in which the upper valley was free of ice.
Leaf fragments that reach the floor of a lake have sometimes fallen from their trees several years, or even decades, before they were buried.
In late spring, meltwater from the slopes around Lake Tarnholm carries more sediment into the lake than the glacier does in late summer.
questions.explanation: Haldor’s hypothesis needs a late-summer glacier flood every year, and the third paragraph says the two-per-year ratio holds even below the ash, more than 1,140 years back. If the glacier is only about 600 years old, that older sediment could not have formed as she proposes, which is C. B is the trap, but missing ash from other eruptions does not challenge the dating of the Ossel ash. A is consistent with her view, D involves errors far too small to matter, and E is compatible with two floods a year.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most undermines the two-floods-a-year hypothesis.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: P2 (the glacier’s late-summer flood) and P3 (the ratio above and below the ash).

breakdown.analysis: What does the hypothesis need? A glacier flood every year for the lake’s whole history, because the doubling holds on both sides of the ash. So find something that removes the glacier for part of that time while the doubling continues. A glacier only 600 years old does exactly that: the 1,814 couplets below the ash, formed 1,140 to 2,050 years ago, would have no second flood to explain them.

choices.note: Consistent with Haldor. It shows multiple couplets per year can happen; it doesn’t challenge her account of why they happen at Tarnholm.
Tempting, because it questions the chronicles. But missing ash from other eruptions doesn’t touch the chemical match and date of the Ossel ash.
CORRECT. No glacier before about 600 years ago means no late-summer flood for the older sediment, yet the doubling holds there too.
Too small to matter. A lag of years or decades can’t close a gap of about 2,050 years.
Compatible. Two floods of unequal size still make two couplets; the hypothesis doesn’t need the floods to be equal.

questions.stimulus: Farmer: Agronomists warn that planting corn in the same field year after year steadily depletes the soil and lowers yields. But my neighbor Tolliver has planted corn in his east field every year for two decades, and last year his harvest there was one of the best in the county. So the agronomists' warning about continuous corn planting is greatly overstated.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the farmer's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: presumes that any farming practice that does not lower crop yields must therefore improve the condition of the soil
treats a single field's experience as if it settled a claim about what generally happens in such fields
fails to consider whether rotating crops in the east field would cost Tolliver more than planting corn there every year
relies on a report of a neighbor's harvest that may have been exaggerated by the neighbor himself
overlooks the possibility that the agronomists' warning concerns some crops other than corn grown in the county
questions.explanation: The farmer rebuts a general warning about what continuous corn planting tends to do with one field that happened to do well; one exception cannot show a general tendency is overstated, which (B) names. (D) is tempting, but it only raises a possibility the argument gives no reason to suspect, and even an accurate report of one harvest would leave the flaw in place.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The agronomists' warning about planting corn year after year is greatly overstated.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Tolliver has planted corn in one field for twenty years; last year that field gave one of the county's best harvests.

breakdown.analysis: So what if one field did fine? One lucky field doesn't tell you what usually happens. Structure: 1. Experts: continuous corn tends to deplete soil and cut yields. 2. Tolliver's one field had a great year. → So the warning is overstated. This is the anecdote-versus-trend flaw (a hasty generalization from one case). It's a classic; know it. It's like: my uncle smoked and lived to 90, so the risks of smoking are exaggerated. We need an answer that says the farmer uses a single case to knock down a general claim.

choices.note: Polar vs. logical opposite. The farmer never says the practice improves soil; he only claims the harm is overstated. 'Not harmful' is not the same as 'beneficial.'
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Since this fertilizer doesn't damage the roots, it must make the plants grow faster.

choices.note: CORRECT. One field doing well says almost nothing about what generally happens across many fields. This is the anecdote-versus-trend flaw.
Wrong dimension. The argument is about soil and yields, not about cost. Cost is never in play.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Planting corn every year is the best choice for Tolliver, since soil depletion is minor. (ignores what rotation would cost)

choices.note: Tempting. Doubting a neighbor's brag feels natural. But nothing suggests Tolliver exaggerated, and even a perfectly accurate report of one harvest can't overturn a general warning. You can't pick an answer on a possibility.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: My cousin says his tomato plants never got blight, so blight must be rare. (trusts a possibly biased report)

choices.note: Wrong group. The warning is explicitly about corn, and Tolliver grows corn. There's no mismatch of crops to overlook.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Experts say wheat drains the soil, but my barley field is fine, so the experts are wrong.

questions.stimulus: Editor: For forty years, the Harlow Courier has printed a weekly list of local court filings. Recently some readers have urged the paper to drop the list, calling it an invasion of privacy. The Courier should keep printing it. Court filings are public records that anyone may inspect, so printing them reveals nothing truly private. Moreover, the list is the only regular source of this information for residents who cannot get to the courthouse.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the editor's argument?
choices: The Courier should continue to print its weekly list of local court filings despite readers' privacy objections.
Because court filings are public records that anyone may inspect, they are not private in any sense at all.
The Courier's weekly list is the best available source of information about local court filings for most residents.
Readers who object to the list on privacy grounds should have no say in the Courier's editorial decisions.
Residents who cannot get to the courthouse have no other way to find out what court filings have been made.
questions.explanation: After a background sentence and the readers' objection, the editor states the position: the Courier should keep printing the list; the public-records point and the only-source point both support it, so (A) is the conclusion. (B) overstates a supporting premise ('nothing truly private' becomes 'not private in any sense'), and (C) turns 'only regular source' into an unsupported ranking.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Courier should keep printing the list of court filings.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Filings are public records, so printing them reveals nothing truly private; the list is the only regular source for residents who can't reach the courthouse.

breakdown.analysis: Does the first sentence matter? No. 'For forty years the Courier has printed the list' is background; ignore it. Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. 1. Filings are public records → printing them reveals nothing truly private. 2. The list is the only regular source for residents who can't reach the courthouse. Both of those answer 'why keep the list?' So the conclusion is the sentence right after the objection: the Courier should keep printing it.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the editor's stated position, and both later sentences are reasons for it.

Tempting. It sounds like the editor's key point, and it's close to a premise. But it stretches 'nothing truly private' into 'not private in any sense,' and even the accurate version is support, not the conclusion.
Unsupported ranking. 'Only regular source for residents who can't get to the courthouse' is not 'best source for most residents.' The LSAT is ultra specific about words like best.
Adds a consequence the editor never mentions. Disagreeing with the objectors is not the same as saying they should have no say.

Too broad. The editor says the list is the only regular source for these residents, not that they have no way at all to learn of the filings. And even the accurate version is a premise, not the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: After the Eastgate branch library began offering Saturday story hours, it lent more children's books in a single year than it had ever lent before. Yet in that same year, for the first time in a decade, Eastgate was not the branch of the city library system that lent the most children's books.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Most of the children who attended Eastgate's Saturday story hours had already had library cards before the program began.
Eastgate's lending of adult fiction declined slightly during the year in which the Saturday story hours were added.
That year another branch doubled its children's collection, and its lending of children's books rose far more than Eastgate's.
Saturday story hours tend to be more popular with families of young children than weekday library programs are.
Children's books lent by Eastgate are, on average, returned later than children's books lent by the other branches.
questions.explanation: The puzzle confuses 'more than before' with 'the most of any branch'; Eastgate can set its own record while another branch grows even faster, which is exactly what (C) describes. (D) explains only the unpuzzling half (why Eastgate's lending rose), and (B) is about adult fiction, the wrong group of books.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Eastgate lent more children's books than ever, but it lost its spot as the branch lending the most children's books.

breakdown.analysis: How can Eastgate lend more than ever and still lose first place? Easy: 'more than before' is a relative word; 'the most' is a ranking against every other branch. This relative-vs-absolute switch is a classic paradox engine; know it. A runner can set a personal record and still finish second. We need an answer that says another branch grew even faster.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether story-hour kids already had cards doesn't explain why another branch passed Eastgate.
Wrong group. Adult fiction isn't children's books. This doesn't touch either side of the puzzle.
CORRECT. Eastgate went up, but another branch went up more and passed it. Both facts now fit.
Tempting. Popular story hours explain why Eastgate's lending rose. But the rise is the half of the puzzle that isn't puzzling; this says nothing about why another branch passed Eastgate.
Wrong dimension. How late books come back has nothing to do with how many are lent.

questions.stimulus: Last quarter, Kerrow Market offered shoppers free samples of its new house-brand granola at the store entrance. Of the roughly 2,000 shoppers who took a sample, 40 percent bought a box of the granola during that same visit. Clearly, then, the sampling stand is an effective way to boost sales of the granola.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Shoppers who took a sample were more likely than other shoppers to describe the store's prices as quite reasonable.
Shoppers who declined a sample tended to spend less in total during their visit than did shoppers who took one.
On those same days, under 5 percent of shoppers who skipped the sample bought a box of the granola.
Shoppers who are never offered free samples at the store sometimes buy food products that they have never tasted.
Throughout the quarter, the granola was priced well below comparable brands of granola sold at the store.
questions.explanation: A 40 percent purchase rate among samplers means nothing without knowing the rate among shoppers who did not sample; (C) supplies that comparison group and shows a huge gap. (E) points the wrong way: a low price is an alternative reason many shoppers bought the granola, so it weakens rather than strengthens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The sampling stand effectively boosts granola sales.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 40 percent of shoppers who took a sample bought the granola that day.

breakdown.analysis: 40 percent compared to what? If 40 percent of shoppers who never tasted it also bought a box, the stand did nothing. The argument looks at only one group. This is the missing-comparison-group flaw; it's everywhere on the LSAT, so know it. It's like saying a tutor works because 80 percent of her students passed, without asking how many students passed overall. We need an answer that says shoppers who didn't sample bought the granola far less often.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Opinions about prices aren't granola sales. This doesn't show the samples made anyone buy granola.
Wrong dimension again: total spending, not granola. And it could just mean bigger spenders like free food. It says nothing about whether sampling caused granola purchases.
CORRECT. This supplies the missing comparison group. 40 percent versus under 5 percent on the same days makes the stand look like it really drives sales.
Wrong group and irrelevant. Shoppers who are never offered samples sometimes buying untasted foods tells you nothing about this stand.

Tempting, because a low price sounds like a reason sales were good. But that's the problem: it's a different reason shoppers bought the granola, competing with the sampling explanation. If anything, it weakens.

questions.stimulus: Each summer, at least a few of the public beaches along the Ottery coast have water that is unsafe for swimming. The Ottery tourism office recommends a beach to visitors only if the office does not know the beach's water to be unsafe. This summer the office recommended every public beach on the coast.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: The tourism office does not test the water at the coast's public beaches before recommending them to visitors.
Most of the beaches that the tourism office recommended this summer had water that was unsafe for swimming.
Beaches known to have unsafe water cannot be recommended to visitors by any organization along the Ottery coast.
This summer at least one beach on the Ottery coast had unsafe water without the tourism office's knowing it.
Unsafe water at a few beaches does not reduce the number of visitors to the Ottery coast enough to concern the office.
questions.explanation: Some beaches had unsafe water this summer, and the office recommended all of them while recommending only beaches it did not know to be unsafe; so at least one unsafe beach was unsafe without the office's knowledge, which is (D). (A) is merely possible: the office may test the water and simply miss a problem.

setup.label: Facts
