setup.text: 1) Every summer, at least a few Ottery beaches have unsafe water; 2) the office recommends a beach only if it doesn't know the beach's water is unsafe; 3) this summer it recommended every beach.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to fully prephrase, but combine the facts and something drops out. 1. This summer, at least a few beaches had unsafe water. 2. Recommended → the office didn't know the water was unsafe. 3. It recommended every beach. Chain: unsafe beach → recommended (3) → office didn't know it was unsafe (2). So unsafe-but-unknown beaches exist. Two facts like these force an existence inference. Watch for answers that guess at why it didn't know, or that inflate 'a few' to 'most.'

choices.note: Tempting. 'They didn't know' makes it feel like they didn't look. But the office could test carefully and still miss a problem. We don't know this.
Too strong. 'At least a few' unsafe beaches says nothing about most of them.
Wrong group and too broad. The rule is about this one office, not every organization on the coast.
CORRECT. Unsafe beaches existed this summer, the office recommended every beach, and it recommends only beaches it doesn't know to be unsafe. So at least one unsafe beach went unnoticed.
Wrong dimension and unsupported. The facts say nothing about visitor numbers or what concerns the office.

questions.stimulus:
Ines: The Ferndale Public Library should keep its reading room open until midnight during exam season. Students need a quiet place to study late that costs them nothing, and the library is the only such place in town.

Daniel: Students do need a quiet, free place to study late. But staying open until midnight would mean paying library staff overtime from an already strained budget. The school district's study hall, which also stays open late and is free, should fill that role instead.
questions.stem: Ines and Daniel disagree over whether
choices: students need a quiet place to study late at night that costs them nothing to use
paying library staff overtime would place a strain on the library's already limited budget
the school district's study hall offers a quieter place to study than the library does
students who study late at night during exam season perform better on their exams
the library should keep its reading room open until midnight during exam season
questions.explanation: Ines wants the reading room open until midnight; Daniel says the study hall should fill that role instead, so they disagree over (E). (A) is the trap: Daniel explicitly grants that students need a quiet, free place to study late, so that is a point of agreement.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ines: keep the library open until midnight; students need a free, quiet late-night spot and the library is the only one.; Daniel: yes, students need that, but overtime strains the budget; the district's free study hall should do it instead.

breakdown.analysis: Where does each speaker say yes and the other say no? To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Daniel's first sentence is a concession: 'Students do need a quiet, free place to study late.' So that's shared ground, not a dispute. Then he rejects Ines's plan: the study hall 'should fill that role instead.' That 'instead' is his no to her yes. We need the library-open-until-midnight point.

choices.note: Tempting, because both speakers talk about it. But that's the problem: they both say yes. Daniel opens by conceding exactly this. Agreement, not disagreement.
Only Daniel speaks to this. Ines never mentions overtime or the budget. One speaker silent means no disagreement.
Neither speaker compares how quiet the two places are. Daniel says the study hall should fill the role, not that it's quieter. Unsupported ranking.
Neither speaker says anything about exam results. Out of scope.
CORRECT. Ines says yes in her first sentence. Daniel says the study hall should fill that role instead, so he says no. One yes, one no.

questions.stimulus: Critic: The Wexford Players' managing director claims that moving the company's season from the downtown hall to the new riverside venue will increase ticket sales, because the riverside venue has ample parking. But city surveys show that theatergoers rarely cite parking as a reason for staying home. Clearly, then, the move will not increase ticket sales.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the critic's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: infers that a claim is false merely because one reason offered in support of that claim is weak
relies on surveys whose respondents may not have been representative of the city's theatergoers in general
presumes, without providing justification, that whatever does not reduce attendance at a theater must increase it
takes for granted that ticket sales are the only reasonable measure of the success of a theater company's season
concludes that the company should not move to the new venue on the basis of evidence about parking alone
questions.explanation: The critic undercuts the director's reason (parking) and then concludes the director's claim is false, but the move could raise sales for other reasons, such as a larger hall or a more attractive location; (A) names this. (E) is tempting, but the critic never says the move should not be made, only that it won't raise sales.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The move to the riverside venue will not increase ticket sales.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The director's reason was parking; surveys say parking rarely keeps people home.

breakdown.analysis: So the parking reason is weak. Does that mean sales won't rise? No. The new venue could sell more tickets for a dozen other reasons: a nicer setting, more seats, a busier neighborhood. You might think the flaw is that the survey is shaky. But even with a perfect survey, the critic only knocks down one reason. Treating a failed argument as proof that its conclusion is false is a classic flaw; know it. It's like: 'You say this restaurant is good because it's cheap? Price doesn't matter, so the restaurant is bad.' We need an answer that says the critic infers falsehood from weak support.

choices.note: CORRECT. The critic shows the parking reason is weak and then concludes the move won't raise sales. A weak reason doesn't make the claim false.
Merely possible. Nothing suggests the surveys were skewed. Even with perfect surveys, the real flaw remains.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: We polled visitors at the opera house, and most prefer opera, so the city's residents prefer opera to musicals.

choices.note: Polar vs. logical opposite, and the critic never reasons this way. Nobody here jumps from 'doesn't reduce' to 'increases.'
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The new lobby won't hurt attendance, so it is sure to boost attendance.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. The debate is about ticket sales only; nobody claims sales are the only measure of success.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The season sold out, so it was an artistic triumph.

choices.note: Tempting. It sounds like the critic's attitude. But the conclusion is only that sales won't rise, not that the move shouldn't happen. It adds a consequence the critic never draws.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Parking won't boost sales, so the company must not move.

questions.stimulus: Climate scientist: For years, the Arvik research station measured air temperature with sensors mounted on the roof of its heated main building. In 2019 the sensors were moved to an open field 200 meters away, and the station's average recorded winter temperature since then has been 0.8°C lower than in the previous five winters. Clearly, heat escaping from the building had been inflating the earlier readings.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the climate scientist's argument?
choices: Sensors mounted on the roofs of heated buildings sometimes record air temperatures that are higher than those of the surrounding air.
The sensors installed in the open field in 2019 are a newer and more sensitive model than those used on the roof.
Summer temperatures recorded at the Arvik station, both before and after 2019, have varied considerably from year to year.
At nearby stations whose sensors were never moved, winters since 2019 have also averaged about 0.8°C colder than the five before.
Several other research stations in the region have also moved their sensors away from heated buildings in recent years.
questions.explanation: The scientist attributes the 0.8°C drop to the move, which requires that winters would not have been colder anyway; (D) shows the same drop at stations that never moved, so the drop is better explained by actually colder winters. (B) is tempting, but a newer model only weakens if we add the unstated assumption that it reads lower.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Building heat had been inflating the old rooftop readings.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After the sensors moved away from the building in 2019, recorded winter averages dropped 0.8°C.

breakdown.analysis: Colder readings after the move. Were winters just colder? If so, the readings would have dropped with or without the move. Structure: 1. Sensors moved from roof to field in 2019. 2. Winter averages since are 0.8°C lower. → Building heat had inflated old readings. It's a before/after causal claim that ignores an alternative cause. We need an answer that says the drop happened anyway, somewhere the sensors never moved.

choices.note: Opposite direction. This makes the scientist's explanation more plausible. It strengthens.
Tempting. A new sensor model sounds like an alternative explanation. But nothing says the new model reads lower; you'd have to assume that. Merely possible.
Wrong group (summer, not winter) and a vague word ('varied'). Year-to-year summer swings don't explain a steady winter drop.
CORRECT. Same drop, no move. The likeliest explanation is that winters really were colder, so the move (and building heat) isn't needed to explain the change.
Wrong group. Other stations moving their sensors tells you nothing about what explains Arvik's numbers.

questions.stimulus: Ostler Hardware is considering leaving its downtown storefront. A store that moves to a shopping center will keep its regular customers only if those customers can easily reach the new location. All of Ostler Hardware's regular customers live downtown, and none of them owns a car. So if Ostler Hardware moves to the Brookfield shopping center, it will not keep its regular customers.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Stores that move to shopping centers usually attract enough new customers to replace the regular customers they lose.
The Brookfield shopping center cannot easily be reached by people who live downtown and do not own cars.
If a store's regular customers can easily reach its new location, the store will keep those regular customers.
Most of the people who shop at the Brookfield shopping center arrive there by car rather than by bus.
Ostler Hardware would lose a substantial amount of money if it moved to the Brookfield shopping center.
questions.explanation: Keep customers → customers can easily reach the new location; so if Ostler's carless downtown customers cannot easily reach Brookfield, Ostler won't keep them, and (B) supplies exactly that link. (D) is the attractive trap: how most Brookfield shoppers arrive is about the wrong group and doesn't establish that Ostler's customers can't get there.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If Ostler moves to Brookfield, it will not keep its regular customers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Keep regulars → regulars can easily reach the new site; Ostler's regulars all live downtown and have no cars.

breakdown.analysis: So the regulars live downtown and don't drive. Who says they can't get to Brookfield? Maybe a bus runs right there. Chain: 1. Keep regulars → regulars can easily reach new site. Contrapositive: can't easily reach → won't keep. 2. Regulars: downtown, no car. Missing link: downtown + no car → can't easily reach Brookfield. Then: can't reach → won't keep. We need an answer that says Brookfield isn't easily reachable for carless downtown residents.

choices.note: Irrelevant and slightly opposite. Replacing lost customers isn't keeping regulars, and it doesn't show the regulars are lost.
CORRECT. Downtown, carless → can't easily reach Brookfield → (contrapositive of the rule) won't keep them. The conclusion follows.

Reverses the conditional. The stimulus says easy reach is necessary for keeping customers; this makes it sufficient. And it's about what happens when they CAN reach the store, which doesn't help prove they're lost.

Tempting. If most Brookfield shoppers drive, it sounds hard to reach without a car. But that's the wrong group, and a bus could still serve downtown. It doesn't guarantee the regulars can't easily get there.
Wrong dimension. Money isn't customers. The conclusion is about keeping regulars.

questions.stimulus: Circulation manager: We surveyed everyone who canceled a subscription to the Valley Herald last year, and 70 percent of them said they had at some point complained to us about late delivery. No other complaint was mentioned by even half of them. Clearly, late delivery is what is driving subscribers away, so improving our delivery service should be our top priority.
questions.stem: The circulation manager's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: takes for granted that subscribers who complained about late delivery did so on more than one occasion
presumes, without providing justification, that improving delivery service would cost less than the revenue it would save
relies on the survey responses of former subscribers, who are likely to feel some hostility toward the newspaper
takes for granted that late delivery is the only problem about which any subscriber has ever complained to the paper
fails to consider how many of the subscribers who did not cancel had also complained about late delivery
questions.explanation: The 70 percent figure only matters relative to subscribers who stayed; if 70 percent of loyal subscribers had also complained about late delivery at some point, complaints don't distinguish cancelers at all, and (E) identifies this missing comparison. (C) is the cynical-narrative trap: nothing indicates the former subscribers misreported their own complaints, which the paper could verify anyway.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Late delivery is driving subscribers away, so fixing delivery should be the top priority.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 70 percent of subscribers who canceled had complained about late delivery at some point.

breakdown.analysis: 70 percent of cancelers complained. How many loyal subscribers complained? If it's also 70 percent, late delivery doesn't separate leavers from stayers at all. Structure: 1. Surveyed only cancelers. 2. 70 percent had complained about delivery. → Late delivery drives people away → fix it first. This is the missing-comparison-group flaw, a cousin of correlation-vs-causation. It's like noticing that 70 percent of people who quit a gym complained about the music, without checking current members. We need an answer that says it ignores the complaint rate among subscribers who stayed.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The argument needs no assumption about repeat complaints; one complaint each is enough for the 70 percent figure.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Every reader who wrote in about typos wrote in angrily, so readers are furious about typos. (assumes each writer complained many times)

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Cost-effectiveness could matter for 'top priority,' but the core gap is causal: nothing shows late delivery causes cancellations in the first place.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Faster trucks would keep subscribers, so we should buy them. (ignores whether trucks cost more than they save)

choices.note: Tempting. 'Bitter ex-customers' is a familiar story. But nothing suggests their answers are false, and whether someone complained can be checked. Even with honest answers, the missing comparison group remains.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Former employees say the manager was unfair, but former employees are always bitter, so the manager was fair.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument doesn't need late delivery to be the only complaint, just the one driving cancellations.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Readers complained about the crossword, so the crossword must be the only thing they dislike.

choices.note: CORRECT. That's the missing comparison group. Without the complaint rate among those who stayed, 70 percent tells you nothing about causes.

questions.stimulus: Two years ago, the Halcyon Line coated the hulls of its six oldest cargo ships with a new drag-reducing paint, hoping to cut fuel costs. Since then, each of these ships has burned substantially less fuel per voyage than it did before. Nevertheless, these six ships still burn more fuel per voyage than any other ship in Halcyon's fleet.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to reconcile the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The new drag-reducing paint has also been applied to several of the cargo ships owned by Halcyon's main competitors.
Fuel prices have risen sharply in the two years since the new paint was applied to the six ships.
Before being painted, the six ships burned far more fuel per voyage than any other Halcyon ship did.
Halcyon plans to retire its six oldest ships and replace them with newer vessels within the next decade.
The paint must be reapplied every few years in order to remain effective at reducing drag on a ship's hull.
questions.explanation: 'Burns less than before' is relative; 'burns more than any other ship' is a comparison to the rest of the fleet; if the six ships started far worse than everything else, a substantial cut can still leave them at the top, as (C) says. (B) is a wrong-dimension trap: fuel prices affect cost, not the amount of fuel burned.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The paint substantially cut each old ship's fuel use, but those ships still burn more fuel per voyage than any other Halcyon ship.

breakdown.analysis: Less fuel than before, yet still the most fuel of any ship? Sure, if they started way higher. 'Reduced' is not 'low.' Watch the switch from a relative word (less than before) to a comparison with others (more than any other ship); it's a classic paradox engine. A 300-pound person who loses 50 pounds can still be the heaviest in the office. We need an answer that says the six ships started far above the rest of the fleet.

choices.note: Wrong group. Competitors' ships don't explain the ranking within Halcyon's fleet.
So? Price changes what fuel costs, not how much fuel a ship burns. Wrong dimension.
CORRECT. A big head start in fuel burn means even a substantial reduction can leave them above every other ship.
Irrelevant future plan. Retirement doesn't explain current fuel use.
Merely possible problem. Even if the paint fades someday, the stimulus says fuel use has already dropped substantially. This doesn't explain the ranking.

questions.stimulus: Researcher: Some argue that the ice cores drilled at the Tarn Glacier last decade are too shallow to reveal anything about climate before the last ice age. That is true, but it misses the point of the project. The cores were drilled to record the past few thousand years, and they record that period in exceptional detail, since their annual layers are thick enough to be counted one by one. So the project should be judged a success.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the researcher's argument by the claim that the cores record the past few thousand years in exceptional detail?
choices: It is supported by another claim in the argument and is offered as support for the argument's main conclusion.
It is the main conclusion of the argument, which the other claims in the argument are offered to support.
It is a claim that the researcher concedes is true but argues is irrelevant to evaluating the project.
It is offered as evidence that the cores also reveal something about the climate before the last ice age.
It is a premise offered in support of the claim that the cores' annual layers can be counted one by one.
questions.explanation: The claim about exceptional detail is supported by the countable annual layers ('since...') and in turn supports the main conclusion that the project should be judged a success, so it is an intermediate conclusion, as (A) says. (E) reverses the direction of support: the countable layers support the exceptional-detail claim, not the other way round.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Tarn Glacier project should be judged a success.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Annual layers can be counted one by one → the cores record the past few thousand years in exceptional detail → that was the project's goal → success. (The 'too shallow' objection is conceded but set aside.)

breakdown.analysis: Which claim gets support, and which claim gives it? Follow the arrows. 1. Annual layers can be counted one by one ('since...') → 2. The cores record the past few thousand years in exceptional detail → 3. That was the project's goal → the project should be judged a success. The 'too shallow' objection is conceded and set aside. A claim that receives support and also gives support is an intermediate (subsidiary) conclusion. We need an answer that says exactly that.

choices.note: CORRECT. It's supported by the countable-layers claim ('since...') and in turn supports the conclusion that the project succeeded.
No. The last sentence, 'the project should be judged a success,' is the main conclusion. The detail claim supports it.
This describes the role of a different claim: the 'too shallow' objection, which the researcher concedes but sets aside. Right passage, wrong target.
Opposite. The researcher agrees the cores reveal nothing about pre-ice-age climate.
Tempting, since it connects the two claims correctly. But it runs the arrow backward: 'since' shows the countable layers support the detail claim, not the other way around.

questions.stimulus: Library policy: A book should be removed from the collection if, but only if, it has not been borrowed in the past five years and either it is in poor physical condition or a newer edition of it is on the library's shelves.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the policy stated above?
choices: The Millbrook library removed a travel guide in good condition that had not been borrowed in six years, because a newer edition of it had been ordered.
The Millbrook library removed a cookbook that had not been borrowed in seven years and whose binding had fallen apart, even though no newer edition was available.
The Millbrook library kept an atlas in poor condition that had not been borrowed in eight years, because a patron had recently asked about it.
The Millbrook library removed a novel in poor condition that had last been borrowed three years ago, since a newer edition was on its shelves.
The Millbrook library removed a biography in excellent condition that had not been borrowed in ten years, because it was the library's least-borrowed biography.
questions.explanation: Removal requires both no borrowing in five years and (poor condition or a newer edition on the shelves); the cookbook meets the five-year test and is in poor condition, so (B) conforms. (A) is the near-miss trap: a newer edition that has only been ordered is not on the library's shelves, so the travel guide fails the second requirement.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Remove ⟺ (not borrowed in 5 years) AND (poor condition OR newer edition on the shelves). If both parts hold, remove; if either part fails, keep.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: The library's judgment must match the policy: a removed book must be (1) unborrowed for 5+ years AND (2) in poor condition OR have a newer edition on the shelves; a kept book must fail one of those parts.

breakdown.analysis: Does each book pass every test? The policy is a two-part gate. 1. Not borrowed in the past 5 years (required). 2. Poor condition OR a newer edition on the shelves (one of these). Both parts → remove. Either part fails → keep. Each trap satisfies only part: a newer edition merely on order, a borrowing three years ago, a book kept when both parts are met, or a ranking ('least-borrowed') the policy never mentions.

choices.note: Tempting. Six years unborrowed, and a newer edition exists. But the edition is only on order, so it isn't 'on the library's shelves,' and the book is in good condition. The 'or' condition is left unmet.

CORRECT. Seven years unborrowed (part 1) and a broken binding (poor condition satisfies part 2). Removal is required, and the library removed it. No newer edition is needed since the 'or' is already met.
Violates the policy. Both parts are met (eight years, poor condition), so the atlas should go. A patron's question isn't a condition the policy recognizes.
Fails part 1. Borrowed three years ago means it has been borrowed in the past five years, so it must stay.
Fails part 2: excellent condition and no newer edition mentioned. 'Least-borrowed' is a ranking the policy never uses.

questions.stimulus: To save on wages, Pellam's Home Supply plans to staff fewer checkout lanes on weekday mornings, when few customers shop. But many of its weekday-morning customers are contractors buying supplies in bulk before work, and contractors are the store's biggest spenders. So the plan risks costing Pellam's more in lost sales than it saves in wages.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Contractors who shop at Pellam's account for most of the store's total sales over the course of a year.
Weekday-morning wages make up the largest share of the labor costs that Pellam's pays its checkout staff.
Customers who shop on weekend afternoons are less bothered by long checkout lines than contractors are.
Pellam's managers have not seriously considered reducing checkout staffing at other times of the week instead.
Longer checkout waits on weekday mornings would lead at least some contractors to buy less at Pellam's.
questions.explanation: The predicted lost sales only happen if the reduced staffing actually drives some contractors to spend less; negate (E) (no contractor would buy less despite longer waits) and the risk disappears. (A) is the too-strong trap: the contractors can be the store's biggest spenders, and losing their business can be costly, without their making up most of total sales.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The staffing cut risks losing more in sales than it saves in wages.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Many weekday-morning shoppers are contractors, the biggest spenders.

breakdown.analysis: Big spenders shop on weekday mornings. So what? Do they actually buy less if the lines get longer? If they wait patiently and buy the same, nothing is lost. Structure: 1. Fewer lanes on weekday mornings. 2. Many of those shoppers are contractors, the biggest spenders. → Risk of losing more in sales than saved in wages. Missing link: the longer waits cause some contractors to spend less. Necessary assumptions are usually modest ('at least some'). Negate each choice and see which one breaks the argument.

choices.note: Tempting. If contractors are the biggest spenders, they sound like most of the business. But being the biggest spenders doesn't mean making up most of total sales, and the argument works either way. Too strong.
choices.negation: Contractors do not account for most of Pellam's total sales. (Losing some of them could still cost more than the wage savings; argument survives.)

choices.note: Unsupported ranking. The argument compares lost sales with the wage savings, wherever those wages rank.
choices.negation: Weekday-morning wages are not the largest share of checkout labor costs. (Doesn't touch the argument.)

choices.note: Wrong group. Weekend shoppers are irrelevant to a weekday-morning plan.
choices.negation: Weekend-afternoon shoppers are not less bothered by lines than contractors. (No effect.)

choices.note: Irrelevant. What managers have or haven't considered elsewhere doesn't affect this plan's risk.
choices.negation: Pellam's managers have seriously considered reducing staffing at other times. (No effect.)

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: no contractor would buy any less, however long the wait. Then there are no lost sales, and the argument collapses.
choices.negation: Longer weekday-morning checkout waits would not lead any contractors to buy less at Pellam's.

questions.stimulus: Every one of the 140 employees of the Danvers customer-service call center completed an anonymous self-evaluation last month. One question asked employees to compare their own patience with callers to that of the center's other employees. Most of the employees reported that they are more patient with callers than most of their coworkers at the center are.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: At least one employee who made that report is not in fact more patient with callers than most coworkers.
Most of the employees who made that report are not in fact more patient with callers than most of their coworkers.
No employee at the center could have known whether he or she is more patient with callers than most coworkers.
Employees who are more patient with callers tend to receive fewer complaints from callers than less patient employees do.
Most of the center's employees are less patient with callers than the center's own training guidelines recommend.
questions.explanation: Fewer than half of a group can each be more patient than most of the others, yet more than half of the center's employees reported being so, so at least one report must be false, which is (A). (B) is the trap: if just over half made the report and just under half are truly that patient, only a few reports are false, not most.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Every employee completed the self-evaluation; 2) most employees reported being more patient with callers than most of their coworkers.

breakdown.analysis: How many people can beat 'most of the others'? Fewer than half. Rank everyone; you have to be in the top half. Yet more than half claimed to be there. So some claims are wrong. Worked example: 100 employees, 60 make the claim. At most 49 can truly beat more than half of the other 99. So at least 11 claims are false. But 11 of 60 isn't 'most.' Spell out the quantifier trap: some claims must be false, not most. Watch for answers that inflate 'some' to 'most' or to 'impossible to know.' The right answer here is dense and sits at (A); don't skim past it.

choices.note: CORRECT. More than half claim a spot that fewer than half can hold, so at least one claim must be false.
Tempting. This is the classic quantity trap. But with 60 claimants and up to 49 true claims, only 11 are false: some, not most.
Too broad: 'could not have known.' Nothing says employees can't know how they compare. Some claims are false, but others could be accurate and well founded.
Adds a consequence never mentioned: complaints. The facts are only about reports and patience.
Wrong standard. 'Not more patient than most others' is about relative ranking, not about a training guideline. Polar vs. logical opposite: not in the top half ≠ below the recommended level.

questions.stimulus: Shipping firms that route cargo through the Corrish Strait rather than around the Kell Peninsula save four days of fuel and crew costs per voyage. Yet many firms still avoid the strait. The most likely reason is that insurers charge far higher premiums for voyages through the strait, enough to wipe out the savings from the shorter route.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: The Corrish Strait is narrower and harder to navigate than most of the other shipping lanes in the region.
Pirate attacks on cargo ships passing through the Corrish Strait have become steadily more frequent over the past decade.
Until insurers raised premiums for strait voyages six years ago, most shipping firms routed their cargo through the strait.
Most of the firms that regularly use the Corrish Strait are considerably larger than the firms that avoid it.
Insurers also charge higher premiums for voyages around the Kell Peninsula during the region's winter storm season.
questions.explanation: If premiums are what keeps firms out, firms should have started avoiding the strait when the premiums appeared; (C) shows the timing matches that mechanism, since most firms used the strait until premiums rose. (B) is tempting because piracy might also raise premiums, but as stated it offers a rival reason for avoiding the strait (danger to ships and crews), so it weakens rather than strengthens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Firms avoid the Corrish Strait mainly because insurance premiums for it are high enough to cancel the time savings.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The strait saves four days, yet many firms avoid it.

breakdown.analysis: Premiums are the 'most likely reason'? Why not danger, narrow channels, or something else? Structure: 1. The strait saves four days. 2. Many firms avoid it anyway. → Because insurers charge premiums that wipe out the savings. A good way to strengthen a causal claim is timing that matches the mechanism: if premiums cause the avoidance, avoidance should start when the premiums started. We need an answer that ties the avoidance to the premiums, not to some other drawback.

choices.note: Merely possible, and it points the wrong way. A hard-to-navigate strait is a competing reason to avoid it. It doesn't tie avoidance to premiums.

Tempting. Piracy might push premiums up, which sounds like support. But as stated it's a separate reason to avoid the strait (danger to ships and crews). You'd have to assume it works only through premiums. It weakens.
CORRECT. The avoidance started when the premiums did. Timing that matches the proposed mechanism is solid support for the causal claim.
Vague and irrelevant. Firm size doesn't say anything about why the smaller firms avoid the strait; it hints at a different explanation, not support for premiums.
Wrong group (the other route) and opposite direction. Higher premiums around the peninsula would make the strait relatively more attractive, deepening the puzzle.

questions.stimulus: Last year, none of the patients at Brightwater Dental whose molars were coated with sealant developed a cavity in a sealed molar. This year, every child patient at Brightwater will have sealant applied to his or her molars. So no child patient at Brightwater will develop a cavity in a sealed molar this year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Last year, every Harmon store that hired security guards reported fewer thefts than the year before. This year, no Harmon store will hire guards. So no Harmon store will report fewer thefts this year.

Last season, no Kessler deckhand who wore the new grip gloves hurt a hand while wearing them. This season every apprentice deckhand will wear them. So no apprentice will hurt a hand while wearing them.
Last year, most newspapers that raised their subscription prices lost subscribers. The Ledger will raise its price this year. So the Ledger will probably lose some of its subscribers this year.

Last year, no Wrenfield runner who trained under the new interval plan was injured during the season. This year the coach wants every runner to stay healthy. So she should require every runner to train under the plan.

None of the tomato plants in Ruiz's garden developed blight this summer, and every one of them had been sprayed with a copper solution in early June. So the spray is what kept all of Ruiz's plants free of blight.
questions.explanation: The original takes a past pattern (no one with treatment T had outcome O), notes that a new group will all receive T, and predicts none of them will have O; (B) matches step for step. (D) is the near miss: it starts from the same kind of past pattern but concludes with a recommendation driven by a goal rather than a prediction about a group already set to receive T.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: No child patient will develop a cavity in a sealed molar this year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Last year no sealed patient got a cavity in a sealed molar; this year all child patients get sealant.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Last time, no one who got T had O; now everyone in group G will get T; so no one in G will have O.

breakdown.analysis: What's the skeleton? 1. Last year, no one who got T (sealant) had O (a cavity in a sealed molar). 2. This year, everyone in group G (child patients) gets T. → No one in G will have O. Match the quantifiers and the conclusion type: none / every / none, ending in a prediction. Kill anything that switches to 'most' or 'probably,' draws a causal conclusion about the past, negates the treatment, or turns the prediction into a recommendation.

choices.note: Polar flip. It says the group will NOT get the treatment and concludes it won't get the result. That's reasoning from the absence of T, not from everyone getting T.

CORRECT. No glove-wearer was injured last season; every apprentice will wear the gloves; so no apprentice will be injured while wearing them. Same none / every / none skeleton, and a prediction of fact.
Close in feel, different in structure. 'Most' and 'probably' for a single paper aren't 'none' applied to a whole group.

Tempting. It opens with exactly the right kind of premise: no one who got T had the bad outcome. But then it switches to a goal and a recommendation ('she should require'). The original predicts a fact about a group that will all get T. Recommendation vs. fact is a different conclusion type.
Different conclusion type. This draws a causal explanation about the past, not a prediction about a new group.

questions.stimulus: Dairy farms in Quill County that switched their herds to locally grown alfalfa last year saw average milk output per cow rise by 8 percent, while farms that kept their old feed saw no change. Therefore, any Quill County dairy farm that switches to locally grown alfalfa can expect its cows' milk output to rise.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: All of the farms that switched last year had been using a low-protein feed that none of the other farms used.
Locally grown alfalfa costs considerably more per ton than the feed that most Quill County dairy farms currently use.
Milk output per cow can be affected by the breed of the cows that make up a dairy farm's herd.
Among the farms that switched to alfalfa last year, the size of the increase in milk output per cow varied considerably.
Cows fed locally grown alfalfa produce milk with a slightly higher fat content than cows given other kinds of feed.
questions.explanation: The argument generalizes from the switching farms to any farm, but (A) shows the switchers differed from the rest: they were leaving a low-protein feed no other farm used, so their gain may reflect escaping that feed rather than any benefit of alfalfa over ordinary feed. (C) is tempting, but it only says breed can matter, not that the two groups of farms differed in breed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Any Quill County farm that switches to local alfalfa can expect milk output to rise.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Farms that switched last year rose 8 percent; farms that didn't switch saw no change.

breakdown.analysis: So the switching farms improved. Will every farm improve? Only if the switchers were like everybody else. What if they started from a worse position? Structure: 1. Switchers' output rose 8 percent. 2. Non-switchers: no change. → Any farm that switches can expect a rise. The comparison group may differ in a way that matters. It's like: patients with a vitamin deficiency felt better after taking the vitamin, so everyone who takes it will feel better. We need an answer that shows the switchers' gain came from something that doesn't carry over to other farms.

choices.note: CORRECT. The switchers weren't typical: they were escaping a poor feed. Their gain may come from dropping that feed, not from alfalfa itself, so a farm already on ordinary feed has no reason to expect a rise.
Wrong dimension. Cost isn't milk output. The argument only claims output will rise, not that switching pays off.
Tempting. Breed really can affect output. But nothing says the switchers and non-switchers had different breeds, so it doesn't explain the gap. Vague word stretched.
So? An average rise of 8 percent is compatible with some farms gaining more and others less. Variation doesn't show the feed didn't cause the rise.
Wrong dimension (fat content, not quantity), and if anything it's a small point in the feed's favor.

questions.stimulus: Dramaturg: Some critics define a 'repertory company' as any theater company that stages several different plays in a single season. But consider a company that stages five plays in a season, hiring a separate cast for each production and never reusing an actor. No one would call that a repertory company, since the hallmark of repertory is a stable group of actors who perform together across productions.
questions.stem: The dramaturg's argument proceeds by
choices: describing a case that clearly counts as a repertory company but that the critics' definition fails to include
arguing that the critics' definition should be rejected on the grounds that few actual theater companies satisfy it
describing a case that satisfies the critics' definition but that clearly does not count as a repertory company
showing that the critics' definition implies that every theater company, whatever its practices, is a repertory company
suggesting that the critics proposed their definition mainly in order to praise companies that they already favored
questions.explanation: The five-play company with a new cast each time meets the critics' definition (several plays in one season) yet is plainly not a repertory company, so the dramaturg shows the definition is too broad, as (C) says. (A) is the mirror-image trap: it describes showing a definition is too narrow (it leaves out a real case), which is the opposite move.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Implied) The critics' definition of a repertory company is wrong: it's too broad.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A company staging five plays with a fresh cast for each meets the definition but isn't repertory, since repertory requires a stable ensemble.

breakdown.analysis: Does the hypothetical company fit the critics' definition? Yes, five plays in one season. Is it a repertory company? The dramaturg says no. Fits the definition but isn't the real thing → the definition is too broad. The opposite move (a real case the definition leaves out) shows a definition is too narrow. Know both; the LSAT loves to swap them. Like defining 'bird' as 'any animal that flies' and pointing to a bat. We need an answer that says: a case satisfies the definition but clearly isn't a repertory company.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the other standard way to attack a definition. But it's the 'too narrow' attack. The dramaturg's company isn't a repertory company and it isn't excluded by the definition. Both halves are backwards.
choices.example: Example of this method: Defining a newspaper as 'a daily printed paper' is wrong, since a weekly town paper is clearly a newspaper yet isn't daily.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. How many companies meet the definition is never discussed; the attack is on accuracy, not popularity.
choices.example: Example of this method: That definition of 'great actor' is useless, since hardly anyone meets it.

choices.note: CORRECT. The company meets the critics' definition (several plays, one season) but clearly isn't repertory. That shows the definition is too broad.
Too broad a claim. One counterexample shows the definition lets in a wrong case, not that it lets in every company. Companies staging a single play wouldn't meet it.
choices.example: Example of this method: If 'athlete' means anyone who moves, then every living person is an athlete.

choices.note: Social-autopilot. Nothing about the critics' motives appears; the dramaturg argues purely from a case.
choices.example: Example of this method: The critics only define 'repertory' that way because their favorite theater happens to fit it.

questions.stimulus: The Climate Data Trust funds a research proposal only if the proposal guarantees that its data will be made public within a year of collection. No proposal that relies on data licensed from a private weather firm can make that guarantee, since such firms restrict publication. Dr. Okafor's proposal on coastal fog relies on data from the Merrin Observatory. So the Trust will not fund Dr. Okafor's proposal.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: If a proposal guarantees that its data will be made public within a year, the Trust will fund the proposal.
Most of the data that the Merrin Observatory provides to researchers is licensed from private weather firms.
Dr. Okafor's proposal does not rely on any data that is already available to the public free of charge.
Private weather firms restrict the publication of all of the data they collect, whether or not it is licensed.
Unless data is licensed from a private weather firm, it is not data from the Merrin Observatory.
questions.explanation: Funded → guarantee; relies on privately licensed data → no guarantee; so the argument needs Okafor's Merrin data to be privately licensed data, and (E), phrased as a contrapositive, says that all Merrin data is licensed from a private weather firm. (B) is the near miss: if only most Merrin data is licensed, Okafor's proposal might rely solely on the unlicensed remainder.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Trust will not fund Okafor's proposal.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Funded → guarantees publication within a year; relies on private-firm licensed data → can't guarantee; Okafor relies on Merrin Observatory data.

breakdown.analysis: Okafor uses Merrin data. Who says that's private, licensed data? Chain: 1. Funded → guarantees publication within a year. 2. Relies on private-firm licensed data → can't guarantee. So: licensed private data → no guarantee → not funded. 3. Okafor relies on Merrin data. Missing link: Merrin data → licensed from a private firm. 'Unless X, not Y' means Y → X: Merrin → licensed private. That's the link, written in contrapositive form. Awkward, but airtight.

choices.note: Reverses the conditional. The guarantee is necessary for funding, not sufficient. And this is about who gets funded, which can't prove Okafor won't be.
Tempting. 'Most' Merrin data being licensed sounds nearly enough. But Okafor might use only the unlicensed part. A sufficient assumption has to guarantee the link, and 'most' leaves a gap.
Wrong group of data. Whether Okafor uses other public data doesn't tell us whether the Merrin data is privately licensed.
Too broad and still missing the link. Even if private firms restrict everything, nothing says Merrin is (or licenses from) a private firm.
CORRECT. Translate: Merrin data → licensed from a private firm. Then Okafor relies on licensed private data → no guarantee → no funding.

questions.stimulus: In March, the Delmont Port Authority began requiring container ships to slow to 10 knots within twenty miles of the harbor. Since then, according to harbor records, there have been no collisions between ships and the whales that feed near the harbor, though there were three such collisions the previous year. Clearly, the speed rule has kept whales from being struck.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: The speed rule is the most effective of all the measures available for protecting the whales that feed near the harbor.
More whales have fed near the harbor since March than fed there during the corresponding months of the previous year.
Container ships obeying the speed rule have not been substantially delayed in reaching the harbor or unloading their cargo.
The lack of collisions since March is not due entirely to there being fewer whales feeding near the harbor.
Whales struck by ships traveling at 10 knots are less likely to be killed than whales struck by faster ships.
questions.explanation: To credit the rule with the absence of collisions, the argument must assume the absence is not fully explained by something else, such as the whales simply being fewer; negate (D) (fewer whales fully explain it) and the rule did nothing. (B) is the too-strong trap: the argument doesn't need more whales than before, only that a decline in whales isn't the whole story.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The speed rule has kept whales from being struck.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Three collisions the year before the rule; zero since the rule began in March.

breakdown.analysis: So collisions stopped. Did the rule stop them, or did something else change? Maybe the whales simply went elsewhere. Structure: 1. Rule began in March. 2. Zero collisions since; three the year before. → The rule prevented strikes. Crediting a policy for an outcome needs the outcome not to be fully explained by something else. We need an answer that rules out an alternative cause, worded modestly ('not entirely'). Test every choice by negating it.

choices.note: Too strong. The rule can have prevented strikes without being the best available measure.
choices.negation: The speed rule is not the most effective measure available. (The rule could still have prevented collisions, so the argument survives.)

choices.note: Tempting, because it's a too-strong version of the right idea. More whales would make zero collisions look impressive, but the argument doesn't need more; it only needs the drop not to be wholly explained by fewer.
choices.negation: It is not the case that more whales have fed there since March. (The same number could be there; the argument still stands.)

choices.note: Wrong dimension: delays, not whale safety. Negating it doesn't touch the conclusion.
choices.negation: Ships obeying the rule have been substantially delayed. (A cost, but the rule could still protect whales.)

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the lack of collisions is due entirely to fewer whales. Then the rule did nothing, and the argument collapses.
choices.negation: The lack of collisions since March is due entirely to there being fewer whales feeding near the harbor.

choices.note: Adjacent scope. The argument is about whether whales are struck at all, not whether they survive a strike. Negating it doesn't matter.
choices.negation: Whales struck at 10 knots are not less likely to be killed. (Irrelevant to whether strikes were prevented.)

questions.stimulus: A piano tuned by the Kestrel Piano Service will hold its tuning for at least six months if it is kept away from radiators. The Morrows' piano was tuned by Kestrel in January, but it sits right beside a radiator in their living room. So the Morrows' piano will not hold its tuning for six months.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: A container shipped by Norrland Freight will arrive within a week if it clears customs on its first inspection. One Norrland container did not arrive within a week. So it did not clear customs on its first inspection.

If a newspaper's investigative series wins a regional award, the paper's circulation rises the following year. The Gazette's circulation rose this year. So its investigative series must have won a regional award last year.

A patron's library card will be renewed automatically if the patron has no overdue fines at renewal time. Mr. Hale is a patron with no overdue fines. So his library card will be renewed automatically.

The new floor cleaner has been shown not to harm hardwood finishes, and anything that does not harm hardwood finishes is safe to use every week. So the new cleaner must actually be good for hardwood finishes.

Any Tallis company apprentice who completes the stage-combat course is cleared to perform fight scenes. Joaquin is a Tallis apprentice who has not completed the course. So he is not cleared to perform fight scenes.
questions.explanation: The argument treats being kept away from radiators as necessary for a Kestrel-tuned piano to hold its tuning, when it was only stated as sufficient (Kestrel tuning and no radiator → holds tuning; the Morrows' piano is near a radiator; so it won't hold), and (E) denies the condition in the same way. (A) is the trap: it mirrors the wording almost exactly but reasons by the valid contrapositive, so it is not flawed at all; (B) is flawed but in a different way (it affirms the result).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Morrows' piano will not hold its tuning for six months.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Kestrel tuning AND kept away from radiators → holds tuning 6+ months; the Morrows' piano was tuned by Kestrel but sits by a radiator.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Members of group G with condition C get result R; this member of G lacks C; so this member won't get R. (Denying the sufficient condition.)

breakdown.analysis: The piano sits by a radiator. Does that doom its tuning? No: staying away from radiators was given as enough for the tuning to hold, not as required. Chain: Kestrel tuning AND away from radiators → holds 6+ months. Morrows: Kestrel tuning, beside a radiator. → Won't hold. That's denying the sufficient condition (mistaking a sufficient condition for a necessary one), a classic; know it. Valid moves: away from radiators → holds (forward), or didn't hold → wasn't kept away (contrapositive). The trap copies the wording but runs the contrapositive, which is valid. We need an answer that commits the same mistake, whatever the wording.

choices.note: Tempting. Same sentence shape: 'will ... if ...', then a fact, then a 'not' conclusion. But it's the contrapositive: didn't arrive → didn't clear customs. That's valid. A valid argument can't match a flawed one.
Flawed, but a different flaw. This reverses the conditional: circulation rose → award, affirming the result instead of denying the condition. Not the same mistake.
Valid. No fines → renewed; Hale has no fines; so renewed. Straightforward application, no flaw.
A different flaw: it treats 'does not harm' as 'is good for' (polar vs. logical opposite). No conditional is being negated.

CORRECT. Tallis apprentice who completes the course → cleared. Joaquin hasn't completed it, so 'not cleared.' Same mistake: the course is sufficient, not shown to be necessary. Different wording ('any ... who'), same skeleton.

questions.stimulus: Media critic: Many people assume that local newspapers are closing because readers now prefer to get their news online. But each of the Fallowmere newspapers that closed this decade had a growing readership, in print and online combined, right up until the year it shut down. What those papers lost was their revenue from classified ads, which moved to free websites. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the media critic's argument?
choices: Fallowmere's newspapers closed because their readers came to prefer getting their news online rather than in print
a local newspaper can survive only if it stops relying on classified advertising for most of its revenue
news that readers obtain from online sources is generally less reliable than news reported by local newspapers
the closures of Fallowmere's newspapers are better explained by a loss of revenue than by a loss of readers
no newspaper anywhere has ever been forced to close because of a decline in the number of people who read it
questions.explanation: The critic pushes back on the popular reader-flight explanation by showing readership kept growing while classified revenue vanished, so the natural completion is that revenue loss, not reader loss, explains the closures: (D). (A) is the trap: it repeats the very popular view the critic is arguing against.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Popular view: papers close because readers moved online; 2) the closed Fallowmere papers had growing combined readership until they closed; 3) they lost classified-ad revenue to free websites.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase word for word, but the direction is clear. 1. Popular view: papers close because readers moved online. 2. The closed Fallowmere papers had growing readership until they closed. 3. They lost classified-ad revenue to free websites. The critic is pushing back on the popular view, so the blank should land where the evidence points: readers didn't leave; money did. When an author pushes back on a popular view, the trap usually repeats the popular view. We need an answer that says revenue loss, not reader loss, explains the closures.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the familiar story. But it repeats the popular view the critic is rejecting; the critic's evidence is that readership kept growing. Social autopilot.
Too strong and adds a consequence. Losing classified revenue hurt these papers, but that doesn't make dropping classifieds the only path to survival.
Wrong dimension. The argument is about why papers closed, not about the quality of online news.
CORRECT. Readership grew while ad revenue vanished, so revenue loss explains the closures better than reader loss. Modest and well supported.
Way too broad. Evidence about Fallowmere this decade can't support a claim about every newspaper ever.

questions.stimulus: The Garrow family papers, recently donated to the county historical society, which plans to catalog them this year, consist mainly of letters. Most of the letters were written by the women of the family, and most of the letters written by the women deal chiefly with household accounts. So most of the letters in the collection deal chiefly with household accounts.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: takes for granted that none of the letters written by the men of the family deal chiefly with household accounts
overlooks the possibility that the women's letters dealing chiefly with household accounts are fewer than half of all the letters
presumes, without providing justification, that letters are a more reliable record of household accounts than ledgers would be
treats the fact that the papers consist mainly of letters as showing that the collection contains no account books
relies on a classification of the letters by subject that historians who study the family might reasonably dispute
questions.explanation: Most letters are by women, and most of those concern household accounts, but 'most of most' can be well under half of the whole (60 percent of letters by women, 58 percent of those about accounts, is about 35 percent of all letters); (B) names this gap. (A) is tempting, but the argument does not need the men's letters to be about something else; if some were about accounts, that would only help the conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most of the letters in the collection deal chiefly with household accounts.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most letters were written by women; most of the women's letters deal chiefly with household accounts.

breakdown.analysis: Most of most is most? Not necessarily. Worked example: 100 letters. 60 by women (most). 35 of those 60 are about accounts (most of the women's letters). That's 35 of 100 letters about accounts: not most. Structure: 1. Most letters → by women. 2. Most women's letters → about accounts. → Most letters → about accounts. 'Most' doesn't chain the way 'all' does; you can only conclude that some letters (in fact, more than a quarter) are about accounts. Know this quantifier trap. We need an answer that says the women's account letters might not reach half of the whole.

choices.note: Not assumed. If some of the men's letters were about household accounts, that would only help the conclusion. The argument doesn't need this, so it isn't the flaw.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Most of the cookbooks were written by women, so no cookbook in the collection was written by a man.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Most of most' can be well under half. If 60 of 100 letters are by women and 35 of those are about accounts, that's 35 of 100: not most. The argument never rules this out.
Wrong dimension. The argument is about what the letters are about, not how reliable they are as records.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The diaries mention prices, so they are a better source for prices than the shop's own ledgers.

choices.note: Never happens. The argument says nothing about account books; 'mainly letters' is just background.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The box is mostly photographs, so there can't be any maps in it.

choices.note: Merely possible. Nothing suggests the classification is doubtful, and even if every label is accurate, the math still doesn't work. Premise objection, not the flaw.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The archivist labeled these letters 'business,' but a historian might call them personal, so the count is wrong.

questions.stimulus: Store owner: Our clothing store has always given full refunds on unworn returns. Lately a few customers have bought expensive dresses, worn them once to an event, and returned them. Some staff want us to stop accepting dress returns altogether. But that would penalize the many honest customers who return dresses that don't fit. Instead, we should accept a dress return only if the original hang tag, which must be cut off before the dress can be worn, is still attached.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the store owner's reasoning?
choices: A store should never change a long-standing policy merely because a few of its customers have found ways to abuse it.
Honest customers should never be made to bear any of the costs that are created by the actions of dishonest customers.
A store's return policy should be designed above all to maximize the store's profits, even at some cost to customer goodwill.
When customers abuse a policy, a store should stop the abuse in a way that preserves the policy's benefits for honest customers.
Customers who are found to have returned merchandise that they have worn should be barred from making any further purchases at the store.
questions.explanation: The owner rejects a blanket ban because it would hurt honest returners and endorses a tag rule that blocks the wear-once abuse while still letting honest customers return ill-fitting dresses; (D) endorses exactly that kind of targeted response. (B) is the strongest trap: it supports rejecting the ban but says nothing in favor of adopting the tag requirement (which itself places a small new condition on honest customers), and (A) would forbid the owner's own policy change.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Rather than banning dress returns, the store should accept them only with the hang tag still attached.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A few customers wear dresses once and return them; a ban would penalize honest customers returning dresses that don't fit; the tag must be cut off to wear the dress.

breakdown.analysis: Why is the tag rule better than a ban? Because it blocks the wear-once trick and still lets honest customers return dresses that don't fit. The owner makes two moves: 1. Reject the blanket ban (it hurts honest returners). 2. Adopt the tag rule (wearers must cut the tag; honest returners don't). A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says, so it must support both moves. We need an answer that says: answer abuse with a fix that stops it without taking the benefit away from proper users.

choices.note: Too strong, and it backfires: the owner IS changing the policy (adding the tag requirement) because of a few abusers. This principle would condemn the owner's own recommendation.

Tempting. It supports rejecting the ban. But it doesn't tell you to adopt the tag rule, and the new tag condition itself puts a small burden on honest customers. Only half the conclusion is justified.
Wrong dimension. The owner reasons about fairness to honest customers, not profit. A profit-first principle might even favor the ban.

CORRECT. It calls for a response that stops the abuse (wearers can't keep the tag) while keeping the benefit for honest customers (ill-fitting dresses still come back). That covers both halves of the owner's reasoning.
Adds a consequence the owner never proposes. Banning abusers isn't part of the plan and doesn't justify the tag rule.
